DecKeywords: Aggravation (preexisting condition); Continuing entitlement; Disc, degeneration (cervical)
DecSummary: Beginning in 1980, the worker experienced neck pain.  In January 1982, he underwent non-compensable surgery for nerve root decompression.  He returned to work in August 1982.  In November 1982, he suffered a further neck injury at work.  The Appeals Adjudicator granted benefits until August 1983.

The worker operated a punch press in order to form parts for aluminum windows.  She experienced pain in her wrist.  The Board granted her benefits but then terminated them on the basis that she was adjudged fit to return to her regular work.

DecKeywords: Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (preexisting condition)
DecSummary: The employer sought SIEF relief in excess of 50%.  The worker, then aged 54, had suffered a compensable injury in 1974 which was diagnosed as left lumbar strain, with possible disc herniation.  The worker returned to work as a steamfitter in 1975 though he continued to experience intermittent symptoms.  In 1979 the worker's condition deteriorated further and he had to stop working.  Surgery was performed later that year to remove a protruding disc.  The worker was granted a 60% pension in 1981.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (altered gait); Continuity (of treatment)
DecSummary: The worker suffered low back, neck, shoulder and foot injuries in 1969 and 1971.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further temporary benefits for the back, neck and shoulder disabilities and denying an increase in the pension the worker received for the foot disability.

The worker appealed the termination of her temporary supplement benefits when she quit a job soldering cables less than three weeks after she started it.  The job was very light, but the worker complained that she could not remain seated for eight hours.  She was receiving a 10% pension for her lower back condition.

The worker suffered a knee injury in July 1983 and a groin injury in May 1984.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying continuing entitlement subsequent to January 1985.  On the evidence, the worker was not disabled by knee, groin or back disabilities subsequent to January 1985.  The worker's major condition during the period in question was urinary incontinence.  The appeal was dismissed.  [8 pages]

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (supplements, temporary) (extension); Supplements, temporary (rehabilitative purpose); Supplements, temporary (wage loss)
DecSummary: The worker appealed the denial of entitlement to continuing wage loss benefits after March 1988.  The worker suffered a back injury in 1980 while employed in a position that required heavy lifting.  After receiving benefits for six months, he returned to work but he had to lay off that job permanently in 1981 at age 33.  He was assigned a pension in 1982 which was currently at the 15% level.

DecKeywords: Intervening causes; Delay (reporting injury); Disablement (repetitive work); Sewing machine operator; Subsequent incidents (outside work)
DecSummary: A sewing machine operator was not entitled to benefits for disabling low back pain.  The onset of pain occurred while bending at home on the weekend prior to the lay-off.  There was no evidence to establish a relationship between her repetitive work activities and the onset of disability.  There was no supporting medical evidence and there was a delay in reporting for six months.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  The Tribunal did not have jurisdiction regarding an earlier claim file since, although the employer explicitly requested access to it, it had not been dealt with by the Board.  It could not be said that the Board implicitly dealt with this file since the existence of different claims implies the existence of two different accidents.

The worker suffered injuries to his knees and right shoulder in 1981.  The accident aggravated pre-existing osteoarthritis.  The Panel found that the worker reverted to his pre-accident state sometime after his return to work shortly after the accident.  The worker was not entitled to benefits for a lay-off in 1985.  That lay-off was related to the non-compensable degenerative osteoarthritic condition rather than to the compensable accident.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of symptoms); Disablement (change in work); Recurrences (compensable injury)
DecSummary: The worker laid off in 1984 with cervical and low back pain.  The worker related the lay-off either to a change in work or to two previous compensable accidents.  The Appeals Adjudicator denied entitlement for the lay-off.

DecKeywords: Pensions (assessment) (dynamic testing) (repetitive strain injury); Pensions (assessment) (enhancement factor); Pensions (assessment) (epicondylitis)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting a 5% pension for right epicondylitis and a 1% pension for a right index finger disability.  In Decision No. 817/89I, the Panel requested a reassessment and submissions from the Board regarding dynamic testing for assessment of repetitive strain injuries.
The worker was a labourer for a meat packing company.  On December 8, 1987, he was working in the freezer area.  The next day he complained of a still neck.  He was off work until March 1988.

DecKeywords: Discretion, Board (pension assessment) (fettering); Pensions (assessment) (tinnitus); Board Directives and Guidelines (pensions) (assessment)
DecSummary: The worker disputed the adequacy of his 2% pension award for tinnitus.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a pension for a wrist disability.  The worker suffered wrist pain from repetitive work and received temporary benefits for about one year.  The worker had preexisting weak wrists.  On the evidence, the worker's preexisting non-compensable condition was aggravated by her work.  This aggravation resolved by the time benefits were terminated.  The inability to return to repetitive work was a reflection of her normal physical limitations.  The appeal was dismissed.  [8 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for one week only for aggravation of her allergic condition.  The worker was a nurse.  In January 1979, she was sprayed in the face with perfume.  She suffered an immediate severe allergic reaction.  In 1981, she left work due to her condition.

DecKeywords: Administrative Fund (transfer of costs); Discretion, Board (rehabilitation); Discretion, Board (supplements, temporary) (part-time work); Significantly greater than is usual; Supplements, temporary (wage loss) (part-time work)
DecSummary: The worker, while receiving full temporary supplementary benefits, found part-time employment.  Initially, he felt there was a good chance of full-time employment.  Although his hours of work did increase, full-time employment did not develop.  The worker continued to look for full-time employment while performing the part-time job and received a wage loss supplement during this time.
A millwright was granted medical aid benefits for hearing loss but was denied a pension for hearing loss and tinnitus.

DecKeywords: Natural justice (opportunity to make submissions); Reconsideration (procedural error)
DecSummary: The worker requested reconsideration of Decision No. 594/89L, in which leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board was denied.  One of the grounds for the leave application was that the worker was denied natural justice when the Appeal Board did not provide him with an opportunity to make submissions on a re-evaluation of his claim by the WCB Pension Section as directed by the Appeal Board.  In Decision No. 594/89L, the Panel found that the worker's submission had merit but that it was common practice for the Appeal Board to proceed in this manner.  The Panel concluded that the practice might have resulted in denial of due process but there was no evidence that the worker was discriminated against or treated unfairly.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (hearing loss) (retroactivity); Hearing loss; Retroactivity
DecSummary: The Hearings Officer found that the worker established entitlement for hearing loss in 1977 and granted medical aid benefits only.  In 1980, an audiogram indicated hearing loss of 40 decibels in one ear and 30 decibels in the other.  In 1988, the Board adopted a new policy on hearing loss that would grant pensions for hearing loss of 35 decibels in one ear and 25 decibels in the other.  The new policy was not made retroactive.

The worker suffered a low back strain in November 1954 in a compensable accident when he had to stop his motorcycle suddenly.  To stop the motorcycle, the worker had to twist his body sharply to the left and shift the weight of the motorcycle to the left side of his body.  He was off work for two weeks.  In 1956, the worker suffered a further back injury when he struck a pothole but benefits were denied.  After increasing pain from 1971 to 1975, the worker underwent a laminectomy and discotomy.  The worker appealed denial of further benefits.

In January 1985, the worker began installing 'H valves' on mini vans.  Each time he leaned forward, he banged his lower abdomen in the groin area on the grill of the van.  In June 1985, the worker began to experience pain in his groin area.  A fibrolipoma was diagnosed in August 1985 and surgically removed in September 1985.
A seamstress suffered a lumbosacral strain in June 1981.  Benefits were denied subsequent to March 1982.  In September 1986, a 15% pension was awarded retroactive to the date of the accident.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  The Panel was satisfied that the employer would not misuse the information.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board which denied entitlement for recurrence of a back disability in January 1985.  The worker was in receipt of a 25% pension and was working part-time.  In January 1985 he stopped working due to back pain.  The worker's doctor submitted reports indicating that the worker was totally disabled.  A WCB doctor, noting the grossly decreased range of movement, agreed.

An adjuvant in a nursing home suffered a back injury in January 1987 while trying to prevent an obese patient from falling.  The Board terminated benefits in November 1987, finding that the worker was fit for regular work.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Cirrhosis (primary biliary); Disablement (exposure); Exposure (trichloroethane); Industrial disease (poisoning) (chlorinated hydrocarbons); Presumptions (industrial disease)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for primary biliary cirrhosis.  The worker used lubricants and solvents containing trichloroethane.  Tests indicated that exposure was minimal and certainly below Ministry of Labour guidelines.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (Board submissions); Epicondylitis; Pensions (assessment) (dynamic testing) (repetitive strain injury)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a finger injury for which he was awarded a 1% pension.  He also received a 5% pension for epicondylitis.  The worker appealed the quantum of the awards and the denial of an enhancement factor.

DecKeywords: Penalties; Board Directives and Guidelines (penalty assessments) (charitable organization)
DecSummary: The employer operated a home for the aged.  The employer appealed a penalty assessment for the years 1983-85.

The Appeals Adjudicator denied benefits beyond a certain date.  The worker's representative intended to argue disability based on organic causes.  The material before the Appeals Adjudicator clearly raised organic and non-organic issues.
The worker's request for partial commutation of his pension in order to have a down payment for a home was denied.
The worker slipped and fell in June 1975 and was off work for about one month.  She returned to work until 1980 when she was laid off.  In 1986, her back condition deteriorated severely.

DecKeywords: Disablement (repetitive work); Fibromyalgia; Sewing machine operator
DecSummary: The worker appealed the denial of initial entitlement for her left shoulder and neck disability which she attributed to her work as a sewing machine operator.  She had worked in a similar capacity since 1974.

DecKeywords: Penalties; Board Directives and Guidelines (penalty assessments) (distortions)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a penalty assessment for the years 1983-85.  The employer submitted that its accident cost history was distorted by three large claims and that it was active in developing safety measures.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work); Independent operator (truck driver); Right to sue
DecSummary: Two plaintiffs were injured in a motor vehicle accident while passengers in a vehicle owned by the employer.  The plaintiffs were proceeding to the employer's remote work site.  The employer provided the transportation.  It was unclear whether workers were paid explicitly for travel time but the Panel was satisfied that the offer of transportation was a benefit to employees which formed part of their remuneration package.

DecKeywords: Arising out of employment (horseplay); In the course of employment (horseplay)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a knee injury.  On the evidence, the worker suffered the injury during a snowball fight at work.  However, there was evidence that snowball fights were a common occurrence during winter at this workplace.  The Panel found that the horseplay leading to the injury was part of the general work environment.  It was a regular occurrence and may have been condoned implicitly by the employer.

A welder fitter suffered a compensable injury in March 1987 when a drill bit went into his hand. The Board discontinued benefits in December 1987. In October 1988, the worker underwent surgery for his hand and in December 1988 benefits were reinstated when the worker laid off due to further hand problems.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for an upper arm injury.  On the evidence, the worker was suffering from deltoid insertion tendonitis related to an accident when the worker was struck on the arm by a heavy basket.  There was a delay in reporting the injury due to gradually increasing pain.  The appeal was allowed.  [5 pages]

The worker suffered a serious low back injury in 1973, for which he was awarded a 30% pension.  In September 1986, while working on his farm, the worker pulled or pushed three or four bales of hay, each weighing between 40 and 50 pounds.  After moving the hay, he experienced an immediate onset of low back pain.

At the worker's request, the Panel clarified Decision No. 111/89, by stating that the decision dealt with organic disability only and that it was open to the worker to pursue entitlement on other bases.  [4 pages]
Access to the worker's file granted to the employer.

The employer applied for an order requiring the worker to attend for a medical examination.  The worker had sustained a shoulder injury while lifting a desk and was in receipt of a 10% pension.  The employer had received 50% SIEF relief but was pursuing an appeal of the level of relief granted.  This constituted a valid compensation goal.

DecKeywords: Case Description; Downside risk; Issue setting; Issue setting (consolidation of issues); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Pensions (assessment) (whole person concept); Reconsideration
DecSummary: A Tribunal decision granted the worker leave to appeal a decision of the WCB Appeal Board which terminated his 10% pension for an emotional disability after two years.  A second Tribunal decision dismissed the worker's appeal on that issue, on the merits.  A third Tribunal decision granted a reconsideration application and ordered that the matter be reopened and that an appeal be heard by a fresh panel.
The worker was involved in a compensable motor vehicle accident in May 1983 and returned to work steadily in July 1983.  In January 1984, the worker laid off due to a mid-back condition.

The worker fell, seriously fracturing his ankle.  Several months later the worker began experiencing low back problems which proved to be disabling.  He had suffered sporadically from back problems for 15 years, but his condition had not been disabling.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (affidavit); Parties (participation)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal a 1975 decision of the Appeal Board which had denied the worker's application for reconsideration of a 1967 decision of the Corporate Board.  The worker was injured in a 1947 compensable accident.  In 1961 his claim for a low back disability was allowed on the basis of an aggravation of his degenerative disc condition.  Benefits were terminated in June 1962.  The Corporate Board's decision denied the worker entitlement for his back disability beyond June 1962.
A welder suffered a low back injury in July 1986.  The Board terminated benefits in October 1986, relying on a medical report that the worker was ready to return to work.

DecKeywords: Rehabilitation, vocational (program not offered by Board)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a rotator cuff tear in November 1983.  The Board granted only 50% benefits from October 1985 to August 1986.

The worker slipped on oil in November 1980 and suffered lumbosacral stress.  The worker complained that he continued to suffer from numbness in his legs and pain in his back.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a permanent disability award for residual organic impairment.

A boiler maker suffered a low back injury in September 1984 when he was rising from a bent position and struck his back.  He returned to light work in February 1986.  In September 1987, he suffered an onset of back pain at home while getting out of bed.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Investigation by Tribunal (inspection); Worker (long term service)
DecSummary: A sewing machine operator suffered a back injury in February 1985.  In February 1986 she returned to work as a floorgirl but laid off after one day.  The worker and employer both appealed the level of temporary benefits from February 1986 to December 1986.

The worker suffered a back injury for which he was receiving a pension.  He retrained as a shoemaker, with the Board's approval.  He started a business but was operating at a deficit.  He requested commutation of his pension, valued at about $44,000, to purchase a truck in order to service surrounding villages, to purchase additional equipment and supplies.

A blacksmith suffered back injuries in 1959 and 1982.  He did not lose any time but performed modified work after the accidents.  After a recurrence in February 1985, the Board granted full benefits until July 1985, when it determined that the major disability was severe osteoarthritis of the hip.
A cook suffered a right shoulder strain from lifting a 100 pound bag of flour in June 1983.  The Hearings Officer denied benefits subsequent to October 1984.

DecKeywords: Commutation (home purchase); Pensions (lump sum) (amalgamation of claims)
DecSummary: The worker was receiving a 10% pension for a right knee disability and a 7 1/2% pension for a left knee disability.  He needed to do exercise but was unable to do it in his apartment because of noise from the equipment.

DecKeywords: Investigation by Tribunal (pre-hearing); Issue setting; Procedure (absent parties)
DecSummary: The worker, who lived out of town, telephoned to say he had forgotten about the hearing.  The Panel would not proceed to a decision on the merits in the absence of the worker, unless there was a clear indication of wilful disregard or abuse of the Tribunal's process.  In this case, it appeared that the worker simply forgot about the hearing.  In addition, there was a reference in a medical report to some memory loss.  The hearing was adjourned.

The worker suffered a low back strain in October 1983.  The worker was now suffering from nephropathy or osteoporosis.  The worker was not entitled to ongoing benefits.  There was a four-year delay in reporting the injury and there was no medical treatment from November 1983 to May 1986.

DecKeywords: Collective agreement; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (federal worker); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (medical examination); Legal precedent; Medical examination (employer request); Merits and justice; Statutory interpretation (incorporation by reference)
DecSummary: The worker was an employee of a federal Crown agency, the employees of which were subject to the Government Employees Compensation Act (Can.).  Section 4(2) of that Act entitles such employees to receive compensation 'at the same rate and under the same conditions' as provided under the compensation law of the province where the worker is usually employed.  The worker filed a claim for compensation.  The employer requested, pursuant to the terms of a collective agreement, that the worker attend a medical examination with a physician of the employer's choice.  The worker did not attend and instead sought a determination, pursuant to s. 21(2) of the Workers' Compensation Act (Ont.), that he did not have to attend the examination.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, P. D. (subsequent disclosure); Consequences of injury (iatrogenic illness) (medication) (nausea)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in 1982.  Because of continuing pain, the worker took substantial doses of analgesics, principally acetaminophen with codeine.  In 1986, the worker began to experience recurrent vomiting.

DecKeywords: Aggravation (preexisting condition) (vascular disease); Benefit of the doubt; Vascular disease
DecSummary: The worker tripped and fell at work on March 31, 1986, injuring her back.  A few days later she began to experience cramping sensations in her lower legs.  On April 26, 1986, she underwent a bilateral femoral embolectomy.  Her vascular condition to deteriorate after the embolectomy.

The worker suffered a low back injury in March 1984, for which he received benefits for organic disability until May 1986.  In May 1986 he was awarded a two year provisional pension for psychotraumatic disability.

DecKeywords: Heart attack; Investigation by Tribunal (pre-hearing); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (access to worker file); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (Tribunal assessor); Medical examination (Tribunal assessor); Presumptions (entitlement) (standard of proof); Procedure (medical examination) (Tribunal assessor)
DecSummary: The dependants of a deceased worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits for the worker's death from a heart attack.

The worker had an asthmatic condition since childhood.  In 1979 she began working with the accident employer, where her work involved the use of solder.  The Board granted benefits for aggravation of the preexisting condition from February 1983 but denied benefits subsequent to September 1985.

The worker began probationary employment with a wire and cable manufacturer on January 30, 1986.  On February 28, he suffered a left hand injury when it got caught in equipment, however, he did not lose any time.  On April 9, his employment was terminated.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (use of material)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  The worker contended that the employer previously misused confidential information by disclosing personnel information to the Board.  Even if this was so, it was an isolated event.  The Panel was satisfied that the employer understood the confidential nature of the medical information to which it was requesting access.

The worker struck his head against scaffolding on December 17, 1986.  He suffered headaches and neck pain, for which he was granted medical aid benefits.  The worker was not entitled to benefits for a lay-off starting January 19, 1987 due to low back pain.  The Panel accepted the opinion of a Board doctor that an extension injury to the cervical spine would not result in a lower back strain.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (contemporaneity); Products liability; Right to sue (remoteness); Supplier of motor vehicle, machinery or equipment; Words and phrases (equipment)
DecSummary: The plaintiff in a civil case was a construction worker who was injured while bolting together steel pieces at a construction site.  The defendant was the supplier of the steel.  The plaintiff alleged negligence regarding a defective weld in the steel.  The defendant brought third party proceedings against the contractor, alleging negligence in the method of erection.  The defendant and third party applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Availability for employment (job search); Permanent disability; Supplements, temporary; Worker (long term service)
DecSummary: A firefighter suffered back injuries for which he was receiving a 10% pension.  In May 1984, he returned to modified work as a dispatcher.  He discontinued this work in June 1984 because of inability to cope with the stress of the job.  The worker was suffering from preexisting non-compensable depression and paranoid schizophrenia.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion)
DecSummary: The Appeal Board granted medical aid benefits for hearing loss and a 2% pension for tinnitus but denied temporary benefits for a lay-off.

DecKeywords: Accident (occurrence); In the course of employment (parking lots)
DecSummary: The worker was entitled to benefits for aggravation of a significant preexisting degenerative back condition.  On the evidence, the injury was work-related.  It occurred either when the worker tripped over a curb in his employer's parking lot, when he lifted a carton of books while loading a truck or as a result of the combination of those two events.  The worker reported the parking lot incident immediately and sought medical attention the same day.  His account of the events remained consistent throughout.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Available employment (offer from accident employer); Overpayment
DecSummary: A labourer fractured his left index finger on October 16, 1986.  He returned to work on December 4, 1986.  The Hearings Officer granted temporary total disability benefits until November 19, 1986.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of treatment); Hearing (splitting) (witness availability); Recurrences (compensable injury) (strains and sprains); Three week rule
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable back strain in 1969.  In 1979 she was involved in a relatively serious motor vehicle accident in which she again injured her back.  The worker claimed entitlement since December 1985 on the basis that the deterioration of her back condition had left her unable to work.

The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying dependency benefits for the worker's death from a heart attack.  The worker was a long distance truck driver.  There was no evidence to establish that long distance truck driving should be considered a stressful job and a precipitator of heart attack or heart disease.  The worker had not been working long hours prior to his death.  The Panel found that the worker's death was not a disablement.

The worker underwent surgery for a compensable inguinal hernia in May 1985.  The worker's job involved lifting tubs which weighed up to 170 pounds.  He returned to work on August 12, 1985 and was assigned his regular duties.  The worker was able to perform his job with the help of co-workers when he was required to lift tubs.
A welder suffered a compensable upper back sprain on April 23, 1986.  The Hearings Officer denied entitlement for low back, right hip and bilateral knee disabilities.

DecKeywords: Dependency benefits; Board Directives and Guidelines (dependency benefits)
DecSummary: In 1979, the worker was awarded a 30% pension for silicosis.  In 1980, the worker died.  The Appeals Adjudicator denied dependency benefits.

The worker suffered a compensable injury which left him a paraplegic and for which he was awarded a 100% pension.  He had received previously several partial commutations and was now requesting full commutation of the remainder pension, valued at about $206,000, for the purpose of purchasing a computer franchise business in Montreal.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (escalation); Earnings basis (maximum); Earnings basis (recurrences)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding the earnings basis for calculation of benefits.  The worker suffered a back injury in 1976.  He returned to work, with various interruptions due to his injury, until 1982 when he left because he could no longer perform the work.  He then operated his own business.  In June 1986, he suffered a further exacerbation of his injury and was granted temporary benefits based on his earnings in 1976 (with one statutory escalation effective January 1986).
The worker was an underground miner involved in drilling activity from 1938 to 1951.  The worker was entitled to benefits for white finger disease.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence)
DecSummary: The worker's widow sought leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board which denied her dependency benefits on the basis that the worker's death by coronary thrombosis did not arise out of his employment.

The worker suffered compensable back strains in 1980 and 1982.  In July 1984 he was laid off by his employer, a janitorial service, and he never returned to work, instead claiming that he was totally disabled.
The worker was momentarily exposed to toxic fumes.  As a result of repetitive vomiting, the worker developed a left inguinal hernia.
The worker suffered a right leg injury in 1966.  In the 1980s, he began to complain of knee pain, diagnosed as osteoarthritis.

DecKeywords: Disability (disabled from working); Disablement (nature of work)
DecSummary: The worker struck her right hip in April 1983.  She was diagnosed as suffering from meralgia paraesthetica, for which she underwent surgery in June 1984.  In June 1985, she laid off with a right groin disability.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (white finger disease); White finger disease; Vibrations (tools)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for white finger disease.  The worker did not meet the exposure requirements of the Board guidelines.  The worker used stoper and jack leg drills but not for two years and not immediately preceding the onset of symptoms.  After working as a miner, he worked as a mechanic and had some further exposure to vibratory tools.  The majority of the Panel found, considering the individual merits and justice of the case, that the worker's condition was related to employment.  The appeal was allowed.

DecKeywords: Aggravation (preexisting condition) (rheumatoid arthritis); Benefit of the doubt
DecSummary: In 1980 the worker suffered a non-compensable right ankle fracture which required surgery.  In 1984 he suffered a compensable injury which was initially diagnosed as rotator cuff tendonitis.  The worker suffered three subsequent periods of lay-off due to rheumatoid arthritis between March 1985 and August 1988.  The issue was whether the preexisting condition of rheumatoid arthritis was aggravated by the compensable accident.  The evidence disclosed that the etiology of rheumatoid arthritis is often an enigma.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (employment relationship); Right to sue; Worker (contract of service) (employment relationship)
DecSummary: The plaintiff's husband was fatally injured in a motor vehicle accident while making deliveries for a courier in February 1986.  He had been involved in a compensable accident in 1985.  At that time, arrangements were made for the plaintiff to take over her husband's shift.  Since October 1985, and at the time of the 1986 accident, pay cheques were made out in the name of the plaintiff, even though the husband had been doing all the driving since December 1985.

A carpenter fell in 1980, suffering a back injury.  In 1983, he underwent surgery for removal of discs at L4-5, for which he received benefits.  In 1984 and 1985, the worker underwent bilateral hip replacement surgery.

The worker injured the left side of his head, neck and shoulder in September 1983.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for right hip, right thigh and low back injuries that the worker claimed he suffered while undergoing treatment at HRC in 1985.

The worker was 15 years old in 1977 when he suffered burns in a flash fire while employed as a cook's helper.  He was awarded a 7% pension for facial disfigurement and a 15% pension for other injuries.
The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 282/89 was denied.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Evidence (admissibility after hearing); Issue setting; Pensions (assessment) (back); Rehabilitation (cooperation); Supplements, temporary; Three week rule (documents)
DecSummary: A bushworker suffered a fractured shoulder and soft tissue injuries to his neck, chest, legs and arm when he was struck by a falling tree in December 1980.  He received full benefits until November 1982 and 50% benefits from November 1982 to March 1983.  He was also awarded a 20% pension.  The worker appealed denial of full benefits from November 1982 to March 1983, a supplement subsequent to March 1983 and an increase in the pension.

A steelworker suffered a compensable cervical strain in July 1978 and returned to regular employment after eight weeks.  He suffered whiplash injuries in two non-compensable motor vehicle accidents in 1981.  In March 1986, he suffered a compensable neck strain and returned to regular employment after four weeks.  In June 1986, he laid off for about one year.

DecKeywords: Construction; Hearing loss; Hearing loss (traumatic); Parties (participation)
DecSummary: A construction worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss, which the worker related to noise exposure or to a head injury suffered in a fall.

The worker suffered a compensable lumbar strain in July 1986.  By February 1987, the back strain had clinically resolved but he continued to complain of pain.  The Board authorized twelve weeks of chiropractic treatment, ending in August 1987.

Relevant documents that were not in compliance with the three week rule were admitted by the Panel.  The documents were records of the worker's job duties and an application for sickness and accident benefits.

The worker was a cleaner in a large building used to repair railway cars.  Noise levels in the building ranged from 64 to 110 decibels and, on a regular basis, between 85 and 90 decibels.  In addition, there was the noise from the machines that the worker used to perform his job.
Access to the worker's file granted to the employer.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for some references to personal information which were not relevant.

The worker was granted a partial commutation of his pension to pay off a bank loan which he had obtained to purchase a truck.  The outstanding balance on the load was $10,800, while the commuted value of the pension was $78,650.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (supplements, older worker); Rehabilitation, vocational (benefit for older worker); Supplements, older worker (age)
DecSummary: The worker sought an older worker supplement pursuant to s.45(7) of the Act.  She was in receipt of a 45% pension, of which 15% related to her back disability and 30% to her non-organic condition.  The worker requested entitlement from the date when her pension was confirmed in December 1984, or alternatively, from April 1985 when s.45(7) came into effect.

The worker suffered a left wrist injury in 1975 and was in receipt of a 5% pension.  In January 1985 he was working at a job which allowed him to use his right hand only when he fell and injured both wrists, his neck and back.  The Hearings Officer found that work offered by the accident employer in September 1985 was within the worker's restrictions.  He relied on the opinions of two doctors that the worker was fit to return to his regular work.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer, dated May 14, 1986, which denied the worker an increase in his 15% pension assessment.  The decision also denied the worker's request for supplementary benefits.  The worker wished to include the issues of psychiatric entitlement in this appeal as well.

The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator.  The issues raised by the worker were continuing entitlement to temporary benefits from September 1982, when temporary benefits were finalized, to February 1983, when a pension was granted, and entitlement to a temporary supplement subsequent to February 1983.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Reconsideration (procedural error)
DecSummary: The worker applied to reconsider Decision No. 753/89, in which the worker's s.77 appeal was dismissed.  That decision was made on the basis of written submission without an oral hearing.  It was the Tribunal's practice to grant an oral hearing for s.77 appeals whenever requested by the parties.  Oral hearings would be requested by making a checkmark in a box on the application form.  In the absence of a checkmark, the parties would be contacted to determine whether an oral hearing was wanted.

DecKeywords: Agreement (parties); Conflict of interest; Issue setting; Notice of hearing; Parties (representation) (conflict of interest); Standing; Withdrawal (of appeal)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for ongoing organic and non-organic disability.  Accidents took place in March 1980, November 1983 and November 1984, each with different employers.  There was also an accident in October 1987, after the decision of the Hearings Officer.  The 1987 employer had not been given notice of the hearing.

A worker with a back disability attended an orthopaedic specialist selected by the employer but did not submit to an examination when a disagreement arose over the taking of facial photographs and signing of some forms.
The worker suffered a neck and shoulder injury in 1977 and a head injury in 1978.
A labourer suffered a low back strain in August 1983.  The Board discontinued benefits in January 1984 after the worker was discharged from HRC to regular employment.
The employer's Section 21 Application, with respect to a worker who had suffered a chest wall contusion and severe back strain, was dismissed.

The worker was a nurse providing home care on a part-time basis.  The worker suffered a compensable back strain in October 1983, for which she lost no time.  In December 1984, she experienced a further onset of back pain.

The worker, aged 37, requested a partial commutation of his pension for the purpose of paying off his house mortgage which currently stood at $43,000.  His 15% pension had a full commuted value of $88,400.  He was earning $33,000 yearly as a salesman, but had a monthly deficit of over $500 which had consumed his cash reserves.  The medical evidence was that a continuing financial problem could prevent him from maintaining his employment and that the granting of a commutation would reduce the effects of his present psychological disability which was related to financial stress.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Reconsideration (consideration of issue); Temporary partial disability
DecSummary: The worker applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 308/89 in which the hearing panel found that the worker was not totally disabled and thus denied him entitlement to temporary total disability benefits.

DecKeywords: White finger disease; Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (documents); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report); Mining (drilling) (diamond); Vibrations (tools)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board which denied him entitlement to benefits for white finger disease on the basis that there was insufficient exposure to hand held vibratory tools.  The worker had worked for more than 30 years as an underground mine diamond driller, however, none of the drills he used were hand held.  The evidence showed that the worker was only exposed to hand vibration for an average of 15 minutes per day.  A report by a Ministry of Labour medical consultant concluded that the worker was exposed to only a low or minimal level of exposure.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion)
DecSummary: There was evidence to support the Appeal Board's decision that the worker was not disabled beyond his pension level during the period in question.

The worker suffered a cervical strain on September 24, 1985.  He received temporary total benefits until December 19, 1985, less time worked during that period.  The worker received chiropractic treatment from September 25, 1985 to January 31, 1986.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (learner); Earnings basis (nominal remuneration); Words and phrases (nominal remuneration); Worker (learner); Worker (probationary employee)
DecSummary: The worker appealed the calculation of his earnings.  He contended that his actual $6.50 per hour wage rate at the time of the accident did not fairly represent his salary, since it was his remuneration only during a training period to become a merchandise manager with the employer, a drug store.  The injury occurred during the worker's three month probationary period.  The employment was terminated shortly after the injury.

The worker suffered a compensable leg injury in January 1985, for which she was off work for about one week.  The worker laid off in August 1986 due to a worsening of her leg injury, resulting in cramping, numbness and the leg giving out at the knee.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence)
DecSummary: The Appeal Board denied continuing benefits for an arm disability, relying on reports of Board doctors and finding that the worker's continuing disability was not organic in nature.  The Panel found that the Board erred in finding there was no organic disability since one of the reports noted neurological deficits that caused the left arm to give way.

A pipe fitter suffered a compensable accident in July 1984 in which he experienced pain in his neck and shoulders.  He lost no time for this accident and did not report until after he discontinued work in March 1987.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work); Personal coverage; Right to sue
DecSummary: The plaintiff was a partner in a business.  In March 1985, he applied for personal coverage.  In September 1985, he was involved in a motor vehicle accident.  In December 1985, he received an invoice from the Board for personal coverage.  The Panel was satisfied that the coverage was effective from the time it was requested and that the invoice covered the time period from March 1985 to December 1985.  Therefore, the plaintiff was a worker within s.1(1)(z).
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for hearing loss.

The employer received a penalty assessment for the years 1980-82.  A further penalty assessment for the years 1983-85 was cancelled by the Board due to the employer's efforts to improve safety and reduce accidents.

DecKeywords: Delay (onset of symptoms); Procedure (witness fees); Recurrences (compensable injury); Second accident
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in November 1976 when he fell from a roof.  On the evidence, the worker was not entitled to continuing benefits for a neck condition.  There was no mention of neck problems until a report in December 1976.  A subsequent report by the same doctor did not mention neck problems.  The first objective medical evidence of neck problems appeared in 1982.

The worker twisted her knee at work on October 25, 1982 and then bumped it against a workbench the next day.  Though both incidents had been reported to the employer on October 27, 1983, the worker did not see a doctor until January 31, 1983 and did not lay off work until February 7, 1983.

The worker suffered a low back strain in January 1987.  He received full benefits until October 1987 when he was discharged from HRC to modified work.  Full benefits were reinstated in March 1988 when the worker advised that he was prepared to look for work.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (multiple appeals); Procedure (access to worker file) (multiple appeals)
DecSummary: The worker appealed two decisions denying his objections to the release of medical documents relating to his compensation claims.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a low back condition.

DecKeywords: Administrative Fund (transfer of costs); Chronic obstructive lung disease; Construction (drilling) (air track); Exposure (dust); Intervenors; Smoking; Medical opinion (chronic obstructive lung disease); Mining; Parties (of record) (previous employer); Pensions (AMA Guides) (respiratory disease); Pensions (assessment) (chronic obstructive lung disease)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD). The worker had been a miner for many years.  Then, he became an air track driller for a construction company.  The construction company was the accident employer.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion)
DecSummary: The Appeal Board denied entitlement, finding that there was no accident in 1977.  There was a two-week delay in reporting the injury and seeking treatment until after the worker's employment was terminated.

The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying dependency benefits for the worker's fatal heart attack.  The worker was a heating journeyman who died while working alone at a work site.  Medical investigations following his death showed that the worker had severe arteriosclerosis and that he died of cardiac arrythmia due to coronary thrombosis.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (health care) (chiropractic) (treatment control); Health care (chiropractic)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying payment for chiropractic treatment after February 1987.  The Hearings Officer determined that continued treatment was supportive only.
The worker suffered a right knee injury in 1974 for which he was awarded a 15% pension.

The worker was off work for five days after November 30, 1981.  The Panel found that the worker did suffer an injury at work on that date despite the absence of a record in the employer's log book, which it was the employer's practice to maintain.  The worker did seek medical attention on that day for an injury which he reported to have been sustained at work.

The employer appealed a decision finding that the worker's upper back, cervical and arm disability of December 1986 was the result of an August 1985 compensable accident which had resulted in a similar disability.

The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the worker's death from a heart attack at work in 1984.  The worker's job duties were modified in 1978 or 1979 to accommodate an underlying heart condition.  The modified work involved distribution of rolls of towelling.  There was some evidence that the worker was instructed not to lift the slings containing the rolls.  However, evidence indicated that he did lift and carry the slings.  The worker suffered the heart attack while lifting.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (altered gait); Continuity (of symptoms)
DecSummary: The worker suffered neck injuries in 1969 and 1971 and a knee injury in 1975.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying continuing entitlement for his neck condition.

A construction labourer suffered compensable back injuries in June 1954, May 1973 and August 1977.  He laid off in May 1978 and has not worked since.  The worker held a number of strenuous jobs between 1954 and 1973.  He had preexisting degenerative disc disease and osteoarthritis.

DecKeywords: Bronchitis; Exposure (isocyanate fumes); Issue setting; Jurisdiction, Board (over own process); Referral to Board
DecSummary: The worker claimed benefits at the Tribunal for chronic bronchitis related to long term exposure to isocyanate fumes.  He also stated that he suffered headaches, nausea and stomach upset from exposure to unknown chemical fumes on January 4, 1984, and claimed benefits for one day when he went to his doctor.

DecKeywords: Pensions (lump sum) (ten per cent pension) (advantage to worker)
DecSummary: A bakery worker suffered a back injury for which she was awarded a 10% pension.  She appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying commutation of the pension.  The worker wanted the pension to buy a vehicle and certain equipment which would assist her in obtaining employment as a dog groomer.

The worker suffered a right knee injury in 1974, for which he was awarded a 20% pension.  In April 1984, the worker was unable to continue working and has been essentially unemployed since that date.  In 1987, the Hearings Officer granted a two year provisional pension for psychiatric disability.  This award was also made retroactive to April 1984.  The worker appealed, claiming the award should have been made retroactive to an earlier date.

The worker suffered compensable back and neck injuries in June 1986.  The worker returned to his pre-accident work from October to December 1986.  His medical condition was the same in July as in October.  The employer had offered the worker his pre-accident job in July, and perhaps modified work.

The worker suffered a back injury, for which he was receiving a 25% pension.  The Panel accepted the evidence of the worker's treating doctor and found that the worker was entitled to temporary total disability benefits from January to June 1985, when he was experiencing a period of acute back pain which rendered him totally disabled.  [5 pages]
The worker, who had a preexisting back condition, suffered compensable back injuries in February 1977 and August 1983.  The worker appealed denial of benefits subsequent to May 1984.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence)
DecSummary: The Corporate Board of the WCB confirmed a worker's entitlement to benefits for an accident in 1968.  The worker was a bushworker working with a skidder owner/operator.  The worker and the owner/operator entered the employer's garage to repair the skidder and the worker was injured by an exploding tire.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Continuity (of treatment)
DecSummary: The worker suffered an injury to his nose in 1978 when a cable struck the worker's hard hat, forcing it down onto his safety glasses.  A laceration to the bridge of the nose was diagnosed.  In May 1988, the worker underwent nasal surgery, including a nasal septoplasty and limited rhinoplasty.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the nasal surgery.
The worker objected to the employer's application for an order requiring the worker to attend for a medical examination.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (recurrences); Temporary disability (beyond pension level)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable back injury in 1975, for which he was awarded a 20% pension.  He experienced a number of recurrences, including a recurrence in December 1986.  After this recurrence, he received temporary benefits until April 1987.

The worker suffered a back strain in September 1969 and was off work until December 1969.  The worker was not entitled to benefits for a lay-off in 1981.  The 1969 accident was an aggravation of preexisting symptomatic spondylolisthesis with spondylosis and disc degeneration.  The disability in 1981 was a natural progression of the underlying condition.  [6 pages]

The worker suffered a shoulder injury in 1973 and a further shoulder injury in 1977.  In 1984, he was awarded a pension retroactive to 1980, which was the date on which shoulder complaints increased.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying arrears to the date of the accident in 1973.
The worker objected to the employer's request that the worker attend a medical examination.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (job search); Rehabilitation, vocational (considering self totally disabled)
DecSummary: The worker suffered an injury in June 1983.  He appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying full benefits from November 1983 to October 1985.

DecKeywords: Degree of earnings impairment (cognitive impairment); Impairment of earning capacity (future wage loss); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Permanent disability (disfigurement); Procedure (referral to Board); Pensions (assessment) (head)
DecSummary: The worker was struck in the head by a crane and suffered a depressed compound left frontal skull fracture.  The worker made a good recovery, but was left with a 17 cm. scar over his left eye.  That eye drooped in comparison with the right eye and there was a definite depression in the mid-forehead.  The worker also experienced headaches, dizziness, short-term memory loss, a reduction in the speed with which he could perform work and other activities, fatigue, occasional blurred vision and increased irritability.  The worker was particularly disturbed and upset about his scar.

The worker suffered a neck injury in May 1978 and received benefits until March 1979.  The Panel found that the worker was entitled to benefits subsequent to March 1979.  The accident aggravated the preexisting but asymptomatic degenerative disc disease.  Since the condition was asymptomatic at the time of the accident, there was no limitation on benefits throughout the period of temporary disability, as provided in the Board guidelines.  [6 pages]

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (disablement); Disablement (vibrations) (vehicular); Vibrations (vehicular); Transportation industry (truck driver)
DecSummary: The worker appealed the dismissal of his claim that his back, neck and jaw disabilities were causally related to his employment.  From 1965 to the late 1970s he drove a loader underground.  That job involved considerable movement of the worker's neck to the left and to the right.  From the late 1970s to 1985, the worker was a truck driver in an open-pit mine.  This job involved considerable jostling and shaking and the worker would often hit his head on the truck's roof, both during the loading and the driving processes.

DecKeywords: Arising out of employment (work relatedness test); In the course of employment (work relatedness test); Second accident; Worker (status) (during medical appointment)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable head injury on September 10, 1986, and returned to work on September 29, 1986.  On December 1, 1986, she went to her family doctor concerning the head injury.  While returning to work after the appointment, she slipped on ice in the street and suffered a wrist injury.  The Board paid for lost time to attend the doctor's appointment but denied benefits for the wrist injury.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt (legal issue); Procedure (reconsideration) (two-step process); Reconsideration (consideration of evidence); Reconsideration (contentious issue); Reconsideration (dissent)
DecSummary: The worker applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 322/89.  In that decision, the worker, who was the captain of a small-town fire department, was denied benefits for stress arising out of his demotion to the rank of first-class fire fighter when the department was merged with that of a larger city.  The majority of the original Panel found that the worker's demotion was not an 'accident' so as to trigger entitlement to compensation benefits.  The Vice-Chair on the original Panel, dissenting, found that the worker had experienced a disablement which arose out of and in the course of his employment.

DecKeywords: Employment (retirement); Temporary partial disability (level of benefits) (retirement)
DecSummary: The worker suffered back and knee injuries for which he was receiving pensions totalling 55%.  He had not worked since 1983.  He was retired by his employer when he turned 65 in 1985.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (short or casual employment); Employment (seasonal)
DecSummary: The worker suffered an accident in December 1981 for which he was awarded a 25% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator regarding the earnings basis for calculation of the worker's pension.

The worker suffered a back injury, for which she was awarded a 15% pension, later increased to 25%.  The worker was not entitled to a higher pension.  The 25% pension was more than adequate in the circumstances.  The worker's doctor was unfamiliar with the nature and purpose of the Rating Schedule.  [7 pages]
The worker, a health care aide, suffered a lumbar strain.  She received temporary total benefits from October 1986 to January 1988, when she was released from HRC as being fit for regular employment.

DecKeywords: Cancer (lung); Exposure (asbestos); Exposure (coal tar emissions); Smoking; Steelworker
DecSummary: A steel foundry worker died in 1970 at age 47 from lung cancer.  Exposure to coal tar emissions and asbestos could have occurred while the worker was working as a brickmason labourer for two years or as a mould sprayer for four different periods totalling less than one year.

DecKeywords: Rehabilitation, vocational (cooperation); Supplements, temporary; Withdrawal (of appeal)
DecSummary: The Panel granted the worker's request to withdraw his appeal regarding commutation of his pension.  The worker had originally applied for the commutation for the purpose of a business investment but was no longer pursuing that business.

DecKeywords: Downside risk; Evidence (inconsistencies) (description of accident); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Mental condition
DecSummary: In October 1984, the worker slipped down some stairs.  He received temporary benefits for two days in October 1984, and for several other periods between January 1985 and April 1986.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying ongoing benefits for organic and non-organic disability subsequent to April 1986.

DecKeywords: Credibility (conflict with other witnesses); Evidence (corroboration); Travel expenses
DecSummary: The worker was entitled to benefits for accidents occurring at work. He had been denied entitlement on the basis of statements of a co-worker who denied knowledge of the accidents.
The worker suffered a sudden onset of pain in her groin while lifting a box at work in July 1983.  The Board denied continuing entitlement for organic and psychological problems.

The worker suffered a neck injury in December 1979.  In October 1980, while at HRC, the worker suffered a low back strain.  The Board accepted the incident as compensable but denied benefits subsequent to the worker's discharge from HRC.

The worker was a dispatcher in the construction industry.  The nature of his position was such that he would be particularly busy between 6:00 and 8:00 a.m., especially in May and June.  The worker suffered chest pains at 7:00 a.m. on June 9, 1981, after lifting two 80-pound bags of cement.  He was unable to return to work because of his heart problems and he died of heart complications in 1988.

The worker suffered a neck injury, for which he was awarded a 25% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits for a low back disability and denying entitlement for chronic pain.

The worker suffered a compensable chest injury, resulting in fractured and separated ribs.  He claimed that shoulder problems experienced subsequent to his return to work were causally related to the compensable injury.

DecKeywords: Class of employer (retail mercantile business); Class of employer (wholesale operation)
DecSummary: The employer objected to its classification as a wholesale operation under Rate #916, claiming that it should be classified instead as a retail mercantile business under Rate #934.  The employer purchased computer accessories from wholesale and manufacturers and sold them to customers such as law firms, accounting offices, government agencies and other businesses.

The worker suffered an injury in June 1958 when he twisted his back.  The original diagnosis was a herniated disc.  A back brace was prescribed and it was paid for by the Board.  The brace was replaced by the Board in 1963.  The worker replaced the brace in 1969 but did not request reimbursement until 1974, at which time the Board refused.  The Board's final decision was made in 1976 but the worker did not appeal to the Tribunal and request further relief until 1987.

The employer's appeal, from the granting of benefits to the worker for a back injury which allegedly arose from a fall at work, was allowed.  The worker's evidence contradicted that of the employer's witness, but more importantly, his own various accounts were inconsistent even with respect to the way in which the  'accident' was said to have occurred.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (temporary partial disability) (Canada Pension Plan); Canada Pension Plan; Rehabilitation (considering self totally disabled) (Canada Pension Plan)
DecSummary: In January 1982, the worker's full compensation benefits under s.41(1)(b) of the pre-1985 Act were reduced to 50% because he was in receipt of Canada Pension Plan benefits.  The worker advised that he would be cancelling his CPP pension as of March 1982 and would be co-operating in a Board rehabilitation program.  He was informed that total benefits would be reinstated as of that date.

The worker's request for reconsideration of Decision No. 349/89R was dismissed.  That decision found no causal relationship between the worker's accident and his right knee disability.  A new medical report submitted by the worker gave an opinion on causation, but it did not provide the background facts necessary to substantiate that opinion and to establish a defect in the original decision.

DecKeywords: Aggravation (compensable injury) (white finger disease); Frostbite; Significant contribution (of compensable accident to subsequent disability); Subsequent incidents (outside work)
DecSummary: The worker suffered from mild white finger disease, for which he was receiving a 5% pension.  The worker suffered frostbite in a non-work-related incident, when he fell, lost consciousness and remained lying on the ground for about 30 minutes.  The temperature was minus 11.5 degrees celcius and snow had recently fallen.
The worker sought a commutation of his 15% knee pension in order to retire a second mortgage on his home in the amount of $20,000.  The commuted value of the pension was almost $24,900.

The worker suffered a low back strain in January 1971.  The Panel found that the worker was not entitled to further benefits, considering the medical reports and lack of continuity of treatment and complaint from 1972 to 1980.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue
DecSummary: The defendant's section 15 application was allowed.
The worker suffered a back injury in June 1984.  On the evidence the worker was not totally disabled in the period from April 1985 to April 1986.  [5 pages]

DecKeywords: Impairment of earning capacity; Significantly greater than is usual; Supplements, temporary
DecSummary: A compensable injury resulted in the amputation of the distal phalanges of the worker's right middle and ring fingers.  He was awarded a 5% pension.  The worker resumed his regular employment as a maintenance mechanic by November 1970.  He continued in that capacity until 1978 when his plant closed down.  The worker claimed that since that time he was unable to find employment in his own field and only worked part-time as a teacher.

DecKeywords: Administrative Fund (transfer of costs); In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work) (employer's vehicle); Overpayment; Time limits (civil action)
DecSummary: The worker's dependants appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the worker's fatal accident.  The worker worked at a remote mining site and stayed in a bunkhouse provided by the employer.  The employer did not provide transportation to the mine site and did not remunerate for travel.  Since the worker's drivers licence was suspended, he asked the job superintendent for a ride home and a ride back to the mine the following week.  The superintendent used a company vehicle.  On the ride back to the mine, the worker was killed in a motor vehicle accident.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The Appeal Board confirmed a 15% pension for the worker's back disability.      A new medical report did not constitute substantial new evidence since the medical facts in the report were known to the Board.

A vehicle service attendant suffered a compensable shoulder injury, for which he was awarded a 10% pension.  In January 1988, he returned to modified work with the accident employer as a parking cashier, at reduced wages.  He was awarded a wage loss supplement from January 1988 to August 1988.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying the supplement beyond August 1988.

DecKeywords: Natural justice (opportunity to make submissions); Reconsideration (error of law)
DecSummary: The worker requested reconsideration of Decision No. 725/89.  In Decision No. 725/89, the hearing panel dismissed the worker's appeal from a decision granting only 50% benefits for temporary partial disability.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (subsequent Board decision)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board which awarded him only 50% temporary partial benefits from March 1976 to March 1977.  The worker was subsequently awarded a 15% lump sum award in recognition of psychiatric entitlement.  The worker had punctured his palm in April 1975.  The wound had apparently healed, but he was unable to return to work.  Functional overlay was observed as early as September 1975 and the worker received psychiatric treatment.  The Appeal Board apparently made its decision solely on the basis of a psychogenic condition, despite the discussion of the diagnosis of reflex sympathetic dystrophy among treating physicians.

The worker was in the process of appealing the denial of her claim for benefits resulting from a disablement.  The Hearings Officer found that there was no relationship between the disability and the work activities.

The worker was struck on the right side of the top of his head by a spray can which fell from a few hundred feet above him.  The worker was granted a 10% pension for a postural vertigo disability, but was denied benefits for neck pain on the basis that it was due to degenerative disc disease.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of complaint); Continuity (of symptoms); Continuity (of treatment)
DecSummary: A police officer injured his lower back in December 1966.  He did not lose any time from work.  In July 1974, he suffered a severe onset of pain at home and, in August 1974, he underwent surgery.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the disability subsequent to 1974.

DecKeywords: Apportionment (standard of proof); Negligence (res ipsa loquitur); Transfer of costs
DecSummary: The accident employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a transfer of costs of an accident to another employer.  A worker was injured when a piece of wood fell from the top of a crane.  The wood was part of a platform built and left in place by the installer of the crane.  It was used during erection and dismantling of the crane but not during operation of the crane.  The piece of wood fell about six months after installation.
A truck driver returned to work on March 14, 1984, after a lay-off for a back problem.  On March 17, he suffered a heart attack at home.  The Hearings Officer denied entitlement for the heart attack.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Rehabilitation, vocational (program not offered by Board); Temporary disability (beyond pension level)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in 1978, for which he was awarded a 20% pension.  After recovering from a non-compensable condition in August 1986, the Board granted 50% temporary partial disability benefits until October 1987, when the pension was increased to 30%.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 30/89 was denied.  The original hearing panel found that the worker's back disability in 1985 was not related to compensable accidents in 1970, 1973 or 1980.  The reconsideration application raised the issue of the relationship of the back condition to compensable accidents prior to 1970.  This was a new issue that had not been considered by either the Board or the original hearing panel.

The worker used vibratory tools continuously from 1955 to 1966 and intermittently from then to 1983.  In 1983, he was diagnosed as suffering from white hand syndrome.  Although Board guidelines require two years of continuous exposure immediately preceding the onset of the disability, the Panel found that the worker was entitled to benefits, considering individual susceptibility.  [4 pages]
The worker suffered a compensable back injury in 1976 for which he was receiving a 10% pension.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  A former employer had a right to continued access with respect to its continuing obligations regarding the worker's compensable injury.

The worker appealed a decision denying the reversibility of his pension.  The worker suffered an accident in 1948, resulting in the amputation of several fingers, for which he was awarded a 15% pension.  The worker routinely asked for cash advances due to extreme financial circumstances.  By 1962, the pension was fully commuted.  In 1976, the pension was increased to 29.5% and in 1982, it was increased to 33%.  In 1987, it was found that the worker's earnings basis had been calculated incorrectly and that monthly payments should have been about $9 more that he received initially.

The worker suffered a minor back strain in June 1977 and received benefits until September 1977.  The worker was not entitled to further benefits.  The degenerative condition in the worker's back was not caused or aggravated by the compensable accident.  [7 pages]
