DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement subsequent to December 1976 for amputation of the worker's right leg.  The worker claimed that the amputation was related to an accident in January 1976 when he fell backwards, catching the calf of his leg in a crevice.

The worker suffered a low back strain in January 1975.  The worker was not entitled to benefits for surgery in 1979 for a prolapsed disc.  The Panel found that the 1975 accident was relatively minor and had resolved by 1976.  There was virtually no continuity of treatment of complaint.  Medical opinion obtained by the Panel indicated that a prolapsed disc caused by an accident would occur shortly after the accident in most cases.  [7 pages]

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (issue in dispute) (relevance) (new information); Procedure (absent parties)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision denying access to medical reports that became available to the WCB after the decision regarding allowance of the claim had been made by the Decision Review Branch.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer allowing the worker's expenses for a medical escort for a trip to Santa Barbara, California.  The Board authorized the worker's examination and operation in California, but the Board's supervisor of health care services had refused the worker's request to pay his wife's expenses.  The worker's wife, who was a registered nurse, nonetheless accompanied the worker.
The appeal by the worker and cross-appeal by the employer were withdrawn.  [3 pages]

The worker suffered a compensable injury in April 1969 when a forklift that he was pulling fell on him.  He found himself in a squatting position, bent forward and down, bearing the weight of the 600 pound forklift.  He received benefits for two weeks, worked for five weeks, then received benefits for another four weeks. No benefits were paid after July 1969.  The worker received no medical treatment between September 1969 and November 1971, when he began to experience disabling problems with his legs and lower back.
A truck driver claimed he suffered a back injury on July 19, 1987, while fixing his truck in Texas.  He continued to work until the end of July and first sought treatment in early August.

The worker was an underground trackman for a mining company.  From 1950 to 1983, he used a pneumatic drill known as an air plugger.  In 1983, the worker was diagnosed as suffering from white finger disease.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (parking lots); In the course of employment (pathways)
DecSummary: The worker slipped and fell while walking on a pathway leading from a parking lot to his employer's premises.  The employer's premises were on the grounds of the Toronto Airport.  The parking lot was owned and operated by the Ministry of Transport, which designated an area for workers of the accident employer.  The accident employer allocated spaces within the area.  The lot was not open to members of the public.  The walkway was the most direct route to the employer's premises.  Maintenance of the lot and walkway was performed by the Ministry of Transport but the accident employer could request that maintenance be performed.

DecKeywords: Impairment of earning capacity; Supplements, temporary
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury, for which he was receiving a pension.  In January 1986, the worker and a partner purchased a business.  The partner left in the summer of 1986.  The worker sold the business in December 1987 for a profit of about $60,000.  The Board paid a supplement until August 1987.  The worker claimed entitlement to a supplement from August 1987 to September 1988.
The worker applied to reconsider Decision No. 756/89L.  The worker submitted new evidence to support entitlement for a knee disability in the form of a letter from a co-worker and a medical report.
The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 839/89 was denied.  The Panel made one minor amendment to clarify the decision.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Board Directives and Guidelines (partial disability benefits) (suitable employment); Epicondylitis; Rehabilitation, vocational (job search)
DecSummary: The worker was entitled to temporary benefits for the period from February to September 1987, as the work that she performed from July 1986 to February 1987 was unsuitable, given the restrictions imposed by her compensable right lateral epicondylitis disability.

The worker suffered a compensable eye injury.  His vision was assessed at 20/400 without correcting glasses and 20/50 with glasses.  The Hearings Officer granted a 2% pension, which is in accordance with the Rating Schedule for 20/50 vision.

The worker was receiving a pension valued at $55,000.  He wanted full commutation of the pension for the purpose of debt liquidation.  Monthly income was about $2,700 and expenses about $2,200 but, because of unexpected expenses, he was near the breaking-point.  Applying the pension to pay off debts, his surplus would rise from $500 to $1,100 monthly.
The worker suffered a low back strain in June 1986 and was off work until July 1986.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for low back disability in 1987.
The worker slipped and fell in September 1985, twisting and injuring his left knee.  He returned to work in January 1986.  In May 1987, he required knee surgery.

A self-employed bricklayer suffered compensable low back strains in January 1975 and May 1975, when he had personal coverage.  He suffered a further low back strain in April 1979, when he did not have personal coverage.
The worker suffered a compensable low back injury in June 1982, for which he was awarded a 10% pension.  The Hearings Officer granted 50% temporary benefits from September 1984 to January 1986.

DecKeywords: Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of issue)
DecSummary: The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying a temporary supplement.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Availability for employment (refusing suitable work) (personal reasons); Supplements, temporary (rehabilitative purpose)
DecSummary: An automotive industry worker suffered a back injury for which she was receiving a 10% pension.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a temporary supplement.

DecKeywords: Arising out of employment (intoxication); In the course of employment (takes self out of employment) (misconduct); Presumptions (entitlement)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for a fatal accident.  The worker was a crew member of a ship.  At the time of the accident the worker was off duty and he had been drinking.  The worker chose to leave the ship by jumping from the rail of the ship onto the dock.  The worker slipped on the dock and fell backwards, struck his head, fell into the water and drowned.  Drinking and jumping from the ship were both violations of the employer's rules.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (use of material)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  There was not persuasive evidence of past misconduct by the employer in dealing with confidential information about the worker.

The worker suffered knee injuries in 1983 and 1986.  The worker's earnings were greater prior to the 1983 accident than the 1986 accident.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer calculating temporary benefits after the 1986 accident on the basis of earnings prior to the 1986 accident.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting benefits to the worker for a blood blister on her finger.  Although the worker could not identify with certainty a specific incident leading to the blister, the Panel was satisfied that an accident occurred at work.  Considering the speed and manner in which the worker was required to carry out her duties, it was likely that a blister could develop and perhaps even go undetected until a later period.  The appeal was dismissed.  [3 pages]

The worker packed vegetables into jars.  She experienced a sudden onset of chest pain on September 10, 1986.  The pain was a muscular sprain which resulted from the nature of the worker's work, which required her to stretch to reach the vegetables.  The worker was entitled to benefits until September 24, 1986.  Continuing disability was not related to the accident but, rather, to a preexisting shoulder condition and to degenerative disc disease.  [6 pages]

The worker was employed as a mobile equipment operator from 1957 to 1985.  Considering the medical evidence and literature, the worker was entitled to benefits for cervical degenerative disc disease.  Vehicular vibration was a significant contributing factor to development of the cervical disability.  Since the condition was permanent, the worker was entitled to a pension assessment.  [11 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  The fact that an employer relationship no longer exists with the accident employer does not bar access under s. 77.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting benefits to the worker.  The worker claimed that he continued to work after being laid off in order to finish what he was doing and that he suffered a pulling injury when the rear wheel of a lift truck became stuck in a crack.

The worker was a truck driver who was exposed to pesticide in January 1980 when a drum broke open.  In February 1980, he was admitted to hospital with symptoms such as nausea, dizziness and extreme fatigue.  He died from leukemia in July 1980.  The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying dependency benefits.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (subsequent disclosure)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  Pursuant to s. 77(3), disclosure of the material, to a representative that the employer may retain, is permitted.

The worker appealed a decision denying him entitlement for a left-sided hearing loss on the basis that it was not causally related to a 1980 compensable head injury.  He also appealed a decision denying him entitlement for a low back disability on the basis that it was not causally related to a compensable accident in 1971.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying commutation of the worker's pension.  The worker was a truck driver who now owned and operated a variety store.  The worker wanted to reduce debts, which would allow him to hire more help, thereby allowing him more leisure time.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (commutation) (ten per cent pension); Pensions (lump sum); Pensions (lump sum) (amalgamation of claims)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying the commutation of his 6% wrist pension.

DecKeywords: Significantly greater than is usual; Supplements, older worker
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back sprain, for which he was receiving a pension.  The worker was not entitled to an older worker supplement to his pension.  On the evidence, the impairment of earning capacity resulting from the compensable disability was not significantly greater than is usual.  The worker was suffering from non-compensable diabetes with resulting severe eyesight problems.  It was this and other non-compensable disabilities which rendered the worker unemployable.  [5 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for bilateral wrist disability.  The worker claimed that he tripped and fell at work on the morning of May 17.  The previous night, the worker was found in the women's washroom at a shopping mall.  While trying to escape from a security guard, he fell down stairs.  The worker was charged and acquitted of fraud regarding his claim.

DecKeywords: Psychogenic pain; Chronic pain; Conversion neurosis; Medical opinion (chronic pain); Psychotraumatic disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered compensable accidents in 1975, 1980 and 1982, for which she was awarded a pension for organic disability.  She appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying temporary benefits subsequent to September 1983 and a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for psychotraumatic disability.

The worker appealed denial of a partial commutation of his pension for the purpose of buying a new car.  The worker had a regular full-time job that was within his capabilities.  He wanted a new car to get to work, especially for the 12 to 15 times per year when he was called at night or on weekends for emergencies.

DecKeywords: Arising out of employment (reasonably incidental activity test); Employer (definition of); In the course of employment (multi-storey buildings); Registration of employers; Right to sue
DecSummary: The employer was a tenant on the second floor of a building.  The worker fell on the stairs leading to the second floor while proceeding to work in the morning.

The plaintiff was a passenger in a truck driven by the individual defendant and owned by the corporate defendant.  The plaintiff and the driver were in the course of employment for the corporate employer at the time of a motor vehicle accident.  The plaintiff's right of action was taken away.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion)
DecSummary: A bartender suffered a compensable shoulder injury for which he was awarded a 6% pension.  The Appeal Board denied a temporary supplement.
The worker's request to reconsider Decisions No. 667/89L and 667/89LR was denied.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (psychotraumatic disability) (five year guideline); Chronic pain; Psychotraumatic disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back injury in 1974, for which she was awarded a 20% pension for organic disability, later increased to 30%.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for psychotraumatic disability.

The worker suffered a foot injury in April 1985 when he stepped on molten glass which punctured and burned his foot.  The Board was considering entitlement for chronic pain but denied continuing entitlement beyond November 1985 for organic disability.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (preparation); Causation (medical evidence) (standard of proof) (stress, mental); Correctional officer (young offenders); Evidence (privacy of worker); Procedure (post-hearing evidence); Stress, mental (standard of proof)
DecSummary: The worker appealed the denial of benefits for an August 1985 lay-off from work which she contended was the result of job-related stress.  The worker had been employed since 1974 in a position that involved the rehabilitation, control, care and supervision of young offenders in a secure custody and detention setting.  The worker contended that the proclamation of the Young Offenders Act (Can.) in April 1985 significantly changed her work environment and contributed to her stress.

DecKeywords: Arising out of employment (employer's premises); Arising out of employment (lunch); Arising out of employment (reasonably incidental activity test); Arising out of employment (recreational activity); In the course of employment (employer's premises); In the course of employment (lunch); In the course of employment (reasonably incidental activity test); In the course of employment (recreational activity)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for an ankle injury suffered while playing volleyball on the employer's premises during an unpaid lunch period.  The game was arranged pursuant to an employer initiative described as a wellness system but participation was voluntary.  The employer was in a remote location, so that, on a practical basis, workers had to remain on the premises during lunch.

DecKeywords: Arachnoiditis; Board Directives and Guidelines (SIEF) (severity of accident); Disc, herniated; Pensions (assessment) (back); Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (preexisting condition)
DecSummary: The worker had back problems at work in March 1972, May 1972 and October 1972.  He laid off work early in November 1972 and returned to work at the end of that month.  In January 1974 the worker again laid off work. Disc herniation was diagnosed and he was never again able to return to his regular work as a welder.  He had back surgery in February 1974 and again in 1981, when untreatable arachnoiditis was diagnosed.  The worker was awarded a 20% pension in 1977, increased to 40% in 1983.  The employer appealed the granting of continuing benefits beyond a 6 to 12 week period.  Alternatively, the employer sought a reduction in the worker's pension rating or SIEF relief.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable minor back strain in 1967.  The Appeal Board denied benefits for a back condition in 1980.  A new medical report related the worker's condition to the compensable accident but it was based on the worker's statements that he had continuing symptoms from 1967.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming the charging of the costs of an industrial disease claim to the employer's accident cost record.  The worker was a refrigeration mechanic who worked for a number of employers from 1958.  In 1985 he died from mesothelioma.  The accident was charged to the accident cost record of the last employer.

Decision No. 434/89I was made into a final decision since the Panel was unable to continue to consider the outstanding, discrete issue.  This decision was made without prejudice to the worker's claim on the outstanding issue.  [2 pages]

The worker suffered a compensable accident in 1964 while working for the first employer.  Shortly afterward, he began to work for a different employer.  In 1982, he was awarded a pension.  The first employer claimed that the permanent disability was related to an accident that occurred while the worker was working for the second employer.

Decision No. 109/89I was made into a final decision since the Panel was unable to continue to consider the outstanding, discrete issue.  This decision was made without prejudice to the worker's claim on the outstanding issue.  [2 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a left inguinal hernia.  The 62 year old worker claimed that he felt a pain while working in November 1987 but did not report an injury.  In January 1988, the hernia was diagnosed during the course of a regular check-up.

The employer appealed a decision confirming the worker's 25% pension award which consisted of 15% for a low back disability and 10% for a neck disability.  The employer objected to any entitlement for a neck disability.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (bias); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (delegation of authority); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (natural justice); Natural justice (opportunity to make submissions); Parties (of record) (previous employer)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board, which denied him entitlement to a supplement from January to May 1978.  The worker had been a miner until a 1972 work accident led to the amputation of his leg.

The worker, a nurse's aide, sought continuing entitlement for a thoracic back disability beyond September 1986, at which time her benefits were terminated.  The injury had occurred in October 1985.  In September 1986, the worker began to provide care in her own home for six children.

DecKeywords: Causation (stress, mental); Stress, mental (effect of disciplinary action); Stress, mental (standard of proof)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for stress.  The worker worked since 1971 as a stenographer.  In the early and mid 1980s, the employer gradually laid off almost half its work force due to economic conditions.  The worker's job was discontinued in 1986 and she was transferred to a different job, which she was unable to do.  After further reassignment and grievances, the worker was given a job in the mail room.  After being spoken to be her supervisor, the worker left work feeling ill and did not return.  The worker's doctor diagnosed her stress condition as anxiety reaction.
A construction labourer suffered a compensable low back strain in June 1965 and returned to work in November 1965.  In 1984, the worker claimed entitlement to further benefits.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (altered gait); Disc, degeneration; Significant contribution (of compensable accident to subsequent disability); Susceptibility
DecSummary: The worker suffered a severe fracture to his right leg in 1959, resulting in leg length discrepancy.  The worker claimed entitlement for lay-offs in 1984, 1985 and 1989 due to degenerative disc disease.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (commutation); Commutation (vehicle purchase)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a right knee injury, for which he was receiving a 12% pension and a pension supplement.  The worker was enrolled in a Board-sponsored retraining programme at a community college, which was 20 miles from his home.  The worker had a car with standard transmission but was no longer able to operate it safely due to his disability.  He requested a partial commutation of his pension to purchase a car with automatic transmission.  The request was denied.  The worker purchased the car with a bank loan.  He completed the course but did not yet have a job.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (health care) (glasses); Health care (glasses)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable accident which required removal of his left eye.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for the purchase of glasses with photogrey lenses.

DecKeywords: Discretion, Board (supplements, older worker); Supplements, older worker (age)
DecSummary: A firefighter suffered a compensable shoulder injury in 1982 when he was 54 years old.  In 1986, he was awarded a 10% pension.
A bus driver suffered a soft tissue injury to his right shoulder and neck in July 1985.  He received benefits until June 1986.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Evidence (privilege)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.
The employer appealed a decision finding that the worker's continuing back problems after 1985 were causally related to his 1978 work injury.

A forester appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for osteoarthritis of the knees.  In the months from September to May, the worker spent 60% - 75% of his time from 1966 to the late 1970s climbing trees using tree spurs.  From then to 1984, he climbed trees 40% - 50% of the time.

DecKeywords: Disablement (repetitive work); Sewing machine operator; Varicose veins; Venous condition
DecSummary: A 38 year old sewing machine operator appealed the decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a venous condition.  The worker laid off in April 1986 with a circulatory problem, originally diagnosed as a thrombosis in the superficial femoral vein of the right thigh.  The worker worked part of the time on a machine that had a mechanical paddle at knee level to raise and lower the head of the machine.  Prior to her lay-off was a very busy period when the worker was working full time on a machine requiring operation of the knee paddle.
The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a penalty assessment for the years 1983-85.

The worker suffered a left ankle injury in 1981, for which he was awarded a 6% pension.  The 1981 accident was treated as an aggravation of a non-compensable 1971 accident.  In 1986, the worker underwent surgery but the Board denied entitlement, relating the surgery to the 1971 non-compensable accident.

The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting benefits subsequent to July 1985.  The worker suffered a shoulder injury in November 1982.  The Board granted benefits until May 1983.  In Decision No. 632, a different Panel of the Tribunal granted benefits until July 1985, making no findings beyond that date.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 121/89 was denied.  There is no obligation on a panel to address all arguments and evidence, although the decision should deal with the major arguments and evidence.  In this case, the hearing panel did not elaborate in its reasons in order to spare the worker's feelings.  Even so, the decision did not fail to address the major arguments and evidence.  [4 pages]

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a bilateral thumb condition.  The worker was a machine operator.  His job required him to grip 300-400 bags per day, make up about 70 cardboard boxes per day and to perform various other activities with his hands.  The original diagnosis was bilateral trigger thumb.  However, some specialists found that the worker was not suffering from this condition.

A welder suffered a low back injury in September 1984.  In March 1985, he was discharged from HRC to modified employment with restrictions against lifting over 10 kilograms.  He returned to modified work for one day before laying off again.

DecKeywords: Causation (heart attack); Exposure (welding fumes); Heart attack
DecSummary: The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying dependency benefits for the worker's death from a heart attack.  The worker was a welder in a mine.  On the day of his heart attack, the worker had to repair a blasting door in a loading pocket of a shaft.  He had to climb 100 feet down to a series of ladders in a manway to reach the loading pocket and a further 20 feet to reach the specific blasting door.  He had to make this climb three times.  Since no ore could be processed through the loading pocket until the repairs were complete, the worker and his co-workers worked through lunch.  In addition, there was no forced air in the area where the worker was working.

A baker's helper suffered a low back strain in October 1986.  He returned to work on March 8, 1987, but laid off again because the job involved extensive bending, twisting and lifting, which was not suitable for his restrictions.  On March 27, 1987, the employer offered the worker a supervisory job which was within his capabilities.  On the evidence, this job offer remained open for the remainder of 1987.  In addition, the worker did not make any serious effort to find alternate work during this period.
The worker suffered a groin injury in 1970.  The worker's estate appealed a decision of the Appeal Board denying entitlement for a low back condition.

An employer appealed the decision of the Hearings Officer granting entitlement for injuries suffered when a cook on a ship fell down stairs.  The cook was a resident employee and fell immediately after completing his shift.
The worker suffered laceration of his left hand in an accident in February 1986.  He received benefits until June 1986.  He also received benefits for surgery in 1987.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The application for leave to appeal an Appeal Board decision which denied the worker entitlement for disablement of his cervical and lumbar spine was dismissed.  The worker was required to bend and reach over a wide table 2,200 times per day.

DecKeywords: Employer (successor rights); Issue setting; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Notice of hearing; Parties (of record); Parties (participation); Procedure (post-hearing submissions)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision denying continuing entitlement.  The worker suffered a compensable injury in 1954 while employed by the City police.  Pursuant to the Municipality of Metropolitan Toronto Act, members of the City police who were so employed at January 1, 1957, became members of the Metro police.  The worker had left the employ of the City police prior to January 1957.  The Board transferred all claims from the City to Metro.  In 1976, the Board held a hearing regarding the worker's claim.  Metro was notified but did not attend.

The worker appealed a decision of the Appeal Board denying entitlement for hearing loss.  The Panel found that the worker was exposed to noise in excess of 100 decibels during 14 months in 1955 and 1956 when he was working as a press operator for a previous employer.  He was also exposed to noise in excess of 90 decibels while working on the soda ash kiln floor of a chemical manufacturer from 1959 to 1978.  The appeal was allowed.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 667/89L was denied.  A new medical report submitted by the worker did not negate the central finding of the Appeal Board denying entitlement on the basis of delay in reporting and seeking treatment.  [5 pages]

DecKeywords: Temporary partial disability; Temporary total disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered a back strain in February 1980.  The Board paid temporary total benefits until March 1982.

DecKeywords: Fibromyalgia; Medical opinion (fibromyalgia); Medical opinion (myofascial pain syndrome)
DecSummary: The worker slipped and fell in September 1982.  She received benefits until June 1984.  In November 1987, the worker died as a result of complications from surgery for a non-compensable condition.  The worker's estate appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying benefits subsequent to June 1984.
The worker's requested to reconsider Decision No. 628/89L was denied.  The Panel's decision not to grant leave to appeal was reasonable in the circumstances.  [4 pages]

The worker suffered a low back strain in July 1978.  In 1982, he was awarded a 10% pension for organic disability and a 15% provisional pension for psychotraumatic disability for 36 months.  The Psychiatric Consultant  recommended review at the end of the 36 months.  The Appeal Board denied continuing entitlement for psychotraumatic disability subsequent to April 1985 without referring the case for a psychiatric reassessment.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a psychological disability resulting from a 1958 accident.  A different claim relating to a 1980 accident had been dealt with by the Claims Review Branch but had not yet been appealed to the Hearings Officer.
The worker suffered a low back strain in 1980 and returned to work after one week.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (cardiac conditions); Heart attack; Medical opinion (heart attack)
DecSummary: The worker's widow appealed a decision denying her dependency benefits on the basis that the worker's heart attack did not result from his employment.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (adequacy of representation); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a depressed skull fracture in November 1941.  The worker was declared fit to return to work and his claim was closed in March 1942.  In May 1942 the worker was killed by a train.  The death certificate recorded the cause of death as shock and suicide.
A foundry worker died of lung cancer.  The issue was whether he had 20 years of work in a foundry, as required by Board policy.

DecKeywords: Allergy (extrinsic allergic alveolitis); Disablement (working conditions) (ventilation system); Industrial disease (characteristic of occupation); Medical report (certainty of diagnosis); Exposure (animals) (pigeon droppings)
DecSummary: The employer appealed the decision of the Hearings Officer finding that the worker's chest disability was the result of exposure to organic dusts which had collected in pigeon droppings in the air vents at the worker's place of employment.  The Hearings Officer accepted a diagnosis of extrinsic allergic alveolitis.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 788/89 was denied.  A new medical report submitted by the worker did not add in any significant way to the evidence which was before the Panel at the time of the original decision.  [3 pages]

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence)
DecSummary: The Appeal Board denied entitlement for a hand disability, and confirmed that decision in a reconsideration.  The Panel found that there was good reason to doubt the correctness of the Appeal Board decision.  On the reconsideration there was substantial new evidence indicating the possibility of an organic hand disability, but this was not definitely and specifically adjudicated upon by the Appeal Board.

The worker was appealing a decision of the Appeal Board denying benefits for a back disability in 1979, which the worker related to a compensable back injury suffered in 1975.  Subsequently, the worker suffered further disabling episodes of back pain in 1983 and 1985.  The 1983 claim was rejected by the Appeals Adjudicator but there had been no final decision of the Board regarding the 1985 claim.

The worker fractured his arm in a compensable accident in April 1986.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement subsequent to March 1987.  In April 1987, the employer offered the worker two modified jobs without wage loss.  The worker rejected one of them.  He performed the other job for about one week until a company-wide two week lay-off.  He did not return to work after the lay-off.
A plumber suffered a heart attack at home.  The Panel found that the worker was not entitled to benefits.
A waitress claimed entitlement for a back disability, which she claimed was related to a fall at work in 1980.  The worker did not report the accident for five years.

The Panel denied the employer's application for an order requiring the worker to attend a medical examination.  The worker had already been examined at least three times by a doctor retained by the employer as its occupational health physician.  Further, the employer had not yet applied for access to the worker's file.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Continuing entitlement; Issue setting
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in October 1984.  He returned to modified work in June 1987 but laid off in July 1987.  He returned again to the same work in September 1987 and worked until December 1987, when he suffered a non-compensable fall.  He also suffered from non-compensable depression in April 1988 and had another non-compensable fall in May 1988.

A cashier began to suffer compensable shoulder, back and neck pain when a ring and bag system was introduced.  The Panel found that the worker was also entitled to benefits for headaches.  There was some medical evidence relating the headaches to muscle spasm.  In addition, a review of the development of the disability showed parallel development of the neck and shoulder complaints and the headaches.

The Board reduced the worker's benefits to 50% after she was discharged from HRC to modified work.  However, there were opinions from a social worker, the family doctor and a visiting registered nurse that the worker was not capable of modified employment.  The Panel found that the worker was entitled to temporary total benefits during the period in question.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Damages, contribution or indemnity; Reconsideration; Right to sue
DecSummary: In Decision No. 226/89, the Panel found that the plaintiff's right of action was taken away against the owner/operator of a truck but that the right of action was not taken away against a trucking company.  In this addendum, the Panel exercised its reconsideration powers to reopen the case to consider the application of s.8(11).  The issue was whether the trucking company was entitled to a declaration under s.8(11) when there had been no finding that it was a Schedule 1 employer.

The worker injured his finger while attempting to pry open his locker at work, in order to get his safety boots.  He had left the key to the locker at home and did not have time to return home to get it.  The employer took disciplinary action by requiring the worker to make restitution for damages to the locker.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying entitlement for a knee disability.  On the evidence, the Panel found that the worker did suffer a knee injury in March 1982.  The worker had a preexisting knee condition.  Although the worker's knee was painful on the day of the accident,  his condition did not worsen as a result.  He was able to continue working for several weeks prior to undergoing knee surgery.  This surgery had been recommended to the worker prior to the accident.
A 75 year old worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying further benefits for hearing loss.  The worker retired in 1976.  The Board awarded a 2.4% pension for hearing loss.

The defendant in a civil action applied to determine whether the plaintiff's right of action was taken away.  The plaintiff went to the defendant hospital to oversee some work.  After completing that work, he walked down the ramp to the hospital's parking lot when the garage door descended and struck him on the head.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion)
DecSummary: The Appeal Board denied entitlement for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.  This is a rare condition existing from birth, which can be made symptomatic by an external event, such as exposure to benzene.  The worker claimed that he was exposed to benzene in a soaking pit area, which contained coke oven gas.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (non-medical information)
DecSummary: Access to the worker file was granted to the employer.  Reports regarding the worker's non-compensable condition were relevant to the issue of SIEF.

DecKeywords: Injuring process; Arising out of employment (remote location); Chance event; Dependency benefits (death results from an injury); Disablement (stress); Heart attack (stress); Injury by accident; Presumptions (entitlement) (standard of proof)
DecSummary: The worker's widow appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying dependency benefits for the worker's death from a heart attack.  The worker was a 62-year-old heavy machinery operator at an isolated work site.  He was last seen alive driving in his truck to the work site.  Six hours later, a co-worker drove by the work site and found the worker's body.
Access to the worker file was granted to the employer.  [3 pages]
The worker suffered tendonitis from repetitive work in 1984.  The Board denied benefits subsequent to June 1986.
The worker fell off a company bicycle in July 1986, hitting his knee.  He did not lay off until one month later.
A carpenter suffered a shoulder injury in February 1987 when a heavy object hit him.  He lost no time from work.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (residual weakness); Subsequent incidents (outside work)
DecSummary: The worker was not entitled to benefits subsequent to November 8, 1984 for a low back disability which he claimed related to a compensable accident of August 1984.

DecKeywords: Earnings basis (period of unemployment); Earnings basis (short or casual employment)
DecSummary: A construction labourer worked from 1972 until 1983, when he was laid off.  On April 18, 1984, he began work with a new employer.  One week later, he sustained a compensable back injury, for which he was awarded a pension.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (issue in dispute) (relevance) (subsequent periods)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for two irrelevant memoranda.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (harmful information)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a compensable shoulder injury in September 1987.  The employer, who requested SIEF relief and disputed payment of continuing benefits beyond 30 days, sought access to the worker's file.  The worker only objected to the release of documents pertaining to his treatment at a behavioural health clinic and of information concerning surgery that he underwent in April 1988.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (job search); Rehabilitation, vocational (cooperation); Temporary partial disability (wage loss benefits)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in January 1982.  He received 50% partial disability benefits for periods subsequent to May 1983.  He was awarded a pension and a supplement in November 1984.

DecKeywords: Impairment of earning capacity; Significantly greater than is usual; Supplements, temporary
DecSummary: The worker was employed as a longshoreman when he sustained a work injury in 1970.  In 1972 he was awarded pensions for his low back and right eye.  Those pensions are currently assessed at 20% and 6% respectively.  The worker received extensive rehabilitation services, including four years of training, as a result of which he worked full-time as a bookkeeper from March 1976 to November 1979.  That job was terminated because he was taking too much time off work due to his back injury.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a low back disability.  On the evidence, the Panel found that an accident did occur in August 1983.  However, the condition resolved within a day or two.  The worker was not entitled to benefits for surgery in February 1984 for a protruding disc.  The subsequent disability and surgery was likely related to progression of an underlying back condition.  The appeal was dismissed.  [8 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a commutation of his pension.  After the hearing but prior to release of the decision, the Panel was informed that the worker had died.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

The worker claimed benefits for a low back and hip disability.  In April 1977 he suffered an acute lumbosacral strain and returned to work in September 1977.  He laid off work because of the pain in 1983.  Examination in 1984 revealed extensive degenerative osteoarthritic changes in the pelvis and hips and there was evidence suggesting an old femoral epiphysiolysis.  A total hip replacement was performed.  With respect to the lumbar spine, there was a slight scoliosis and early degenerative changes were noted in the discs and apophyseal joints.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (issue in dispute) (relevance)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer, except for references to non-compensable disabilities.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (natural justice); Natural justice (disclosure of evidence); Natural justice (opportunity to make submissions)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal an Appeal Board decision which denied him benefits for a low back disability.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical literature)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal an Appeal Board decision which granted him benefits for frost bite only from February 13 to 18, 1965.  He referred to several articles written about frost bite injuries which it was submitted were new evidence unavailable at the time of the hearing.

The worker suffered head and shoulder injuries, for which he was receiving a pension valued at $103,000.  The worker required a partial commutation of $25,000 in order to emigrate to Ecuador, his home country, and buy a home.

DecKeywords: Chronic pain; Issue setting; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (leave to appeal); Psychotraumatic disability; Significant contribution (of compensable accident to development of condition)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a minor back strain in May 1978 and she received benefits from June to August 1978.  The Appeals Adjudicator ruled that the worker was not entitled to further benefits since she did not continue to suffer from any organic disability and there was no psychogenic or psychological disability which resulted from the accident.  The Appeal Board confirmed the Adjudicator's decision.  The worker appealed to the Tribunal for ongoing entitlement on the basis of psychotraumatic disability.
The worker appealed denial of his request for partial commutation of his pension.  The pension was valued at $45,000.  The worker had debts of about $21,000 resulting from a failed business venture.

The worker appealed the 3% pension awarded for his right hand disability caused by tendonitis due to operation of an air gun.  Four surgical procedures failed to correct the worker's problems but he was able to return to full-time modified work that did not involve the use of vibrating tools or heavy gripping with his right hand.

The worker's lawyer requested an adjournment due to the absence of the worker at the worker's appeal.  The lawyer's office had communicated with the worker the morning of the hearing and he had indicated that he would attend.  The lawyer was unable to contact the worker during a half hour delay in the hearing.  An adjournment had been granted to the worker three months earlier.

DecKeywords: Intervening causes; Rehabilitation, vocational (job search); Second accident; Worker (status) (during job search)
DecSummary: The worker suffered an injury when she fell while on the premises of a prospective employer.  At that time, she was conducting a job search in order to maintain entitlement to the temporary supplement being paid to her by the Board.  The Board denied benefits on the basis that she was not a 'worker' under the Act at the time of the fall and because the injury sustained did not result from the worker's compensable disability.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (application of Board policy)
DecSummary: The Appeal Board denied continuation of the worker's provisional pension for psychotraumatic disability, without following the WCB policy to refer the file for psychiatric reassessment.  This was a breach of a safeguard which the WCB had carefully put in place to ensure that any adjudicative body had the benefits of current expert medical opinion prior to termination of a provisional award.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (stress, mental); Disability (disabled from working); Heart condition (stress)
DecSummary: The worker sustained a knee injury in 1975.  He received full compensation benefits for 10 of the next 15 years and was in receipt of a pension.  The worker claimed that he developed a low back condition while being treated for his knee disability.  He also alleged that his cardiac condition, which resulted in by-pass surgery, was due to emotional strain as a result of his compensable injury.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (distinct departure test); In the course of employment (lunch); In the course of employment (personal activity); In the course of employment (travelling); Right to sue
DecSummary: The worker arranged with his employer to combine his two paid 15 minute breaks with his unpaid 30 minute lunch, so that he would have 60 consecutive minutes during which he could eat lunch and do personal banking.  The worker then agreed, as a favour to the employer, to certify a customer's cheque at another bank located in the same mall as the worker's bank.  After lunch, the worker was to proceed directly to a customer's home to perform a service call.  Performing service calls formed part of the worker's regular duties, but certifying cheques did not.

The worker, a punch press operator, fractured his wrist in December 1985.  He returned to his regular work in January 1986, but had to lay off two weeks later due to the increased pain in his wrist.  He had not returned to work since that time.  The employer claimed that the worker was not entitled to benefits for the period from April 1986 to April 1987.

DecKeywords: Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Procedure (absent parties); Temporary partial disability
DecSummary: As the worker had been admitted to a hospital emergency ward the morning of the hearing, and as there was sufficient documentary evidence available, the Panel granted the worker's representative's request to proceed in the absence of the worker.  The employer had chosen not to participate in the hearing.

The worker appealed the level of his pension.  As a result of a crushing injury, the worker was left without a small finger.  He also lost part of the corresponding metacarpal, the bone in the palm of the hand which connected to the small finger.  The worker had been granted a 2% award for the finger and 0.5% for the metacarpal.

The worker suffered a back injury in 1976, for which she was awarded a 10% pension in 1977, increased to 15% in 1982.  The worker appealed denial of a temporary supplement subsequent to 1982.  The employer appealed the pension level.

The claimant for compensation benefits appealed a decision which found that he was not a worker under the Act and therefore was not entitled to benefits.  The claimant was a motor route driver for a newspaper business.  He picked up newspapers at press time and delivered them to various locations.

The worker suffered a head injury in 1969.  He received temporary benefits for various periods.  In 1977, he was awarded a 10% provisional pension for psychotraumatic disability.  The worker appealed denial of continuing temporary disability benefits and denial of a further pension for psychotraumatic disability.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Procedure (Practice Direction No. 9)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying continuing entitlement for a psychotraumatic disability.

DecKeywords: Chronic pain; Maximal medical rehabilitation; Pensions (assessment) (mental condition)
DecSummary: The Hearings Officer granted the worker a 50% pension, including 25% for aggravation and magnification of the residual organic disabilities by the worker's underlying psychological condition.  The Hearings Officer also denied entitlement for chronic pain and granted temporary benefits from November 1987 to June 1988.

A 39 year old carpet installer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a heart attack.  On the day the heart attack occurred, the worker and a co-worker unloaded three rolls of carpeting each weighing 100 to 125 pounds.  They had to carry the carpeting a greater distance than usual.  To install the carpet, the worker spent several hours hammering spikes into concrete stairways.  While carrying some carpet up stairs, a piece of the carpet became stuck.  The worker wrenched it free and experienced an immediate onset of pain.
The Appeal Board denied an increase in the worker's 4.2% pension for hearing loss.  The worker claimed an additional allowance for speech discrimination difficulties.

The worker suffered a lumbosacral strain in September 1976.  The presence of degenerative disc disease was confirmed shortly thereafter.  The worker received benefits from September to October 1976 and from January to March 1977.  In November 1982, while working as a bricklayer, the worker experienced renewed low back pain.  The Tribunal found, in Decision No. 173/87, that there was no relationship between the 1976 accident and the 1982 lay-off.  The worker now claimed for benefits on the basis that he suffered a disablement arising out of his employment on November 17, 1982.

The worker suffered a compensable lumbosacral strain.  He returned to modified work in June 1987.  The work consisted of picking up litter with a stick that had a nail on the end.  The worker was instructed by the employer that he could work at his own pace, taking breaks as required.  In July 1987, the worker had to lay off work due to worsening back problems caused by the fact that he had to walk on rough terrain involving small ditches and inclines.  In November 1987, the worker returned to the same work, but with the further modification that he was not required to walk on rough terrain.  The worker has been employed at this job since then, without further complications.
The worker suffered a low back strain in June 1987, for which he was off work for two weeks.  In April 1988, he suffered an onset of low back pain at home.

The worker slipped in 1979, striking his mouth against a machine.  He received benefits for about one week.  The worker was not entitled to benefits for a neck condition or headaches in 1987.  There was no indication that the worker suffered a neck injury in the accident.  The worker's condition was due to degenerative cervical disc disease.  The accident was not a significant contributing factor to the worker's condition.  [5 pages]

The worker claimed he suffered a back injury on August 4, 1986, when a hook struck him on the back.  There was a delay in seeking treatment and reporting the injury, although not a long delay.  The Panel could not accept the explanation for delay that the worker was concerned for his job, since the worker had a four-day lay-off immediately after the accident, during which he could have sought treatment privately.  The worker's evidence was not sufficiently credible to overcome negative inferences from his failure to report and seek treatment.  [8 pages]
The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 786/89 was denied.  In that decision the Panel granted entitlement but limited benefits to two weeks.

DecKeywords: Heart attack; Smoking; Medical opinion (heart attack) (respiratory disease)
DecSummary: The worker's widow appealed the denial of dependency benefits.  The worker was a miner who for 30 years spent most of his time doing underground drilling and blasting.  The worker died of a heart attack, but an autopsy also revealed that he suffered from emphysema and longstanding lung disease.
The employer appealed the Hearings Officer's granting of benefits for a back condition which resulted from the worker's fall from a bulldozer in May 1983.

DecKeywords: Rheumatoid arthritis; Exposure (methyl ethyl ketone); Presumptions (entitlement)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for rheumatoid arthritis.  The worker related the condition to work he did during one shift when he applied a mixture of resin and hardener to fibreglass.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (admission of evidence); Three week rule
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision regarding the earnings basis for calculation of benefits.  Less than three weeks before the hearing, the employer submitted documents and notified the Tribunal of witnesses to support its position that the worker was not a management trainee.  Previously, this had not been disputed by the employer.

DecKeywords: Aggravation (preexisting condition) (disc, degeneration) (cervical); Disablement (vibrations) (vehicular); Vibrations (vehicular); Transportation industry (truck driver)
DecSummary: The worker drove heavy trucks over crushed rock roads for 13 years, driving 75 to 100 miles per shift.  He was exposed to significant vibration and bouncing in this job.  In January 1983, after lifting a heavy piece of equipment and while pounding with a sledgehammer, the worker experienced numbness in his neck and arms.  Within a month the numbness turned to severe pain and headaches.  X-rays showed gross spondylitic changes in the worker's cervical spine.  The worker did not work thereafter.

DecKeywords: Chronic pain; Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of evidence); Psychotraumatic disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered back injuries in 1969 and 1972 for which he was awarded a 30% pension.  The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board confirming the 30% pension and appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits for chronic pain.
The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a foot condition.

The worker underwent surgery for bilatel inguinal herniae in November 1973.  He claimed that the herniae were related to a lifting incident at work in July 1973.  He did not submit a claim until 1983.

A tree cutter appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying ongoing benefits subsequent to March 1983.  The worker was struck on the right side of his head by a falling tree in July 1982.  The Hearings Officer found no organic or psychological cause for ongoing complaints of head pain and dizziness.

DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the WCB Appeal Board which denied him ongoing entitlement to benefits after June 1981.

The worker suffered a compensable back injury in October 1980.  He received benefits until his discharge from HRC in May 1981 on the basis that he was fit to return to his pre-accident job in concrete forming construction.  The worker claimed that a severe onset of pain while getting out of bed one morning in August 1981 was the result of the 1980 accident.
The worker suffered a compensable neck sprain in August 1982.  He returned to work in February 1983.  In November 1983, he laid off due to low back pain.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer to calculate the worker's pension on the basis of earnings at the time of his first compensable accident in 1963.  There was an onset of back pain in July 1963 for which the worker was off work for six months, an uncorroborated incident in 1967 for which he was off work for three months, an onset in June 1974 for which he received benefits until the end of August 1974, an onset in August 1977 for which he was off work for one week, an onset in October 1978 for which he was off work until January 1979 and another onset in November 1980.  He returned to light work in April 1981, experienced more pain in May 1981 and laid off again in October 1981.  In August 1983, he was awarded a pension.

The worker attended a medical examination requested by the employer with an orthopaedic surgeon.  The orthopaedic surgeon recommended a CAT scan and a bone scan but the worker objected to these tests.

DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement; Medical report (opinion of Board doctor preferred); Reconsideration
DecSummary: The worker's request for reconsideration of Decision No. 915/89 was denied.  The worker was unhappy with the Panel's acceptance of the Board doctor's opinion (which stated that it was unlikely that the worker's degenerative disc disease was a consequence of the compensable accident) over that of his family doctor (which did attribute the degenerative changes to the work accident).

The worker received benefits for a few weeks in January and February of 1979 for a cut right index finger which became infected.  His job involved dipping his hands alternately in very hot and very cold water.  The worker began to complain of right hand problems including loss of sensation in some fingers, with pain radiating to the shoulder when the hand was immersed in cold water.  The worker sought continuing benefits for the period from August 1979 to August 1980.

The worker suffered a compensable left ankle injury when a case was thrown against her left ankle in June 1982.  In September 1986, she suffered a further ankle injury when a box was pushed against her left ankle.  She received benefits after the second accident until August 1987.

The worker suffered back and leg injuries in 1972 and 1982 for which he was awarded pensions totalling 25%.  The worker was not entitled to temporary benefits from December 1986 to October 1987.  Medical evidence supported the conclusion that the worker's condition did not worsen temporarily during this period.  [4 pages]

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory; Medical report (payment for)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

The worker injured his left shoulder at work in September 1986.  In January 1987, he stopped working due to shoulder pain.  In February 1987, he underwent surgery to remove a pin inserted after a non-compensable shoulder dislocation in March 1984.  The worker's condition did not improve after removal of the pin.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (contemporaneity); In the course of employment (personal activity); Right to sue
DecSummary: The plaintiff slipped and fell while attending a conference on the defendant's premises.  The plaintiff's job involved liaising between disabled clients and potential employers.  The curriculum of the conference on the day of the accident dealt largely with technology in the workplace and its application to blind people but also included items of more general interest.  Although attendance at the conference was not required, the Panel found that the plaintiff was in the course of employment.

An assembly line worker suffered back and arm injuries when she fell in February 1986.  On the evidence, the worker continued to be partially disabled by rotator cuff tendonitis subsequent to September 1986.  Two modified jobs offered by the employer were within the worker's medical restrictions and suitable.  The worker was not entitled to full benefits subsequent to September 1986.  [8 pages].

DecKeywords: Abuse of process; Aggravation (preexisting condition) (degeneration) (knee); Estoppel; Out of province; Parties (of record)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting benefits for a knee disability from December 1982 to August 1983 but denying benefits thereafter.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (residual weakness); Overuse syndrome
DecSummary: A laboratory technician lacerated her left ring finger in August 1973.  In 1977, she underwent surgery to her left shoulder related to the compensable accident.  In 1978, she developed osteoarthritis of the right hand.  The Hearings Officer denied entitlement for the right hand disability on the basis that she did not overuse her right hand after the accident.
The worker suffered a compound fracture of his right leg, for which he received benefits.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a left knee disability.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of treatment); Jurisdiction, Board (reconsideration of Appeal Board decision)
DecSummary: A health care aide in a nursing home suffered compensable back strains in March 1979, July 1979 and August 1981.  In June 1982, she began to experience increased pain and laid off in November 1982.  The Appeal Board denied entitlement for the disability in 1982 but the Committee to Review Appeal Board Decisions revoked the Appeal Board decision and granted entitlement.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (consideration of issue)
DecSummary: The Appeal Board granted entitlement for aggravation in November 1976 of a congenital hip condition but discontinued benefits in July 1977.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (conditions of access); Access to worker file, statutory (use of material)
DecSummary: Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.  The worker was concerned that the employer would misuse the information since the employer had released a report received through a previous access request to a prior employer.  The worker and employer agreed to a condition that the reports be released to, and kept in possession of, the employer's solicitor.

The worker suffered a low back injury as well as bruised ribs and hips and burns to his chest and upper arm in December 1973.  The worker was not entitled to continuing benefits for low back, groin and hip problems.  Medical evidence did not establish that ongoing disability was attributable to the 1973 accident.  The weight of evidence suggested that the worker was unable to do heavy work because of his physical stature, not because of residual effects of the accident.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer confirming a 10% pension.  At the hearing, it became apparent that the worker was not disputing the correctness of the Hearings Officer's decision but, rather, was claiming that her condition had deteriorated since that decision.

DecKeywords: Supplements, temporary (rehabilitative purpose); Transitional provisions (commencement); Transitional provisions (retroactivity)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision which denied him entitlement to ongoing supplementary benefits.  The worker injured his back in January 1984 and was awarded a 10% pension in December 1984.  He received a pension supplement for most of the period between February 1985 and February 1988, when benefits were discontinued.

The worker suffered a shoulder injury in 1977 when he was struck by falling equipment.  The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a cervical disability and denying entitlement for shoulder surgery in 1985.

A tree cutter suffered a shoulder injury when he was hit by a tree in July 1984.  The Hearings Officer denied temporary total disability benefits from September 1985 to November 1985 and denied pension supplementary benefits subsequent to November 1985.

DecKeywords: Board Directives and Guidelines (cardiac conditions) (unusual physical exertion); Heart attack (stress)
DecSummary: The worker experienced an onset of cardiovascular symptoms in December 1981 at his home.  He was diagnosed as having had a myocardial infarction.  The worker laid off and then returned to work on February 1, 1982.  He laid off again on February 19, 1982.  He returned to work in April 1982 and continued to work until March 1983 when his cardiac symptoms returned.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (altered gait); Pensions (assessment) (enhancement factor); Pensions (assessment) (knee)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a left knee injury in March 1980, for which he was awarded a 12% pension.  The Hearings Officer denied entitlement for back and right knee disability and denied a temporary supplement.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 865/89 was denied.  The worker disagreed with the decision but did not show any significant defect in administrative process or content of the decision.  [4 pages]
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

Since a compensable fall in January 1985, the worker had complained of migraine headaches, low back pain, neck pain and right upper arm and shoulder pain.  Extensive medical examinations and tests disclosed no significant organic problem.  In July 1988 the worker was awarded a 20% provisional pension for chronic pain.  The Board paid for her chiropractic treatments up to July 1986 only.  The worker sought reimbursement for further treatment taken up to May 1987 ($1009).  She also wanted to undergo further treatment.  The Board refused further payment due to the lack of long-term improvement and the opinion that the treatments reinforced the worker's belief in her disability.
Access to the worker's file was granted to the employer.

The worker's job involved the repetitive lifting, twisting and grinding of various automotive parts weighing from 2 to 26 pounds.  A prior compensable right elbow condition caused him to work primarily with his left elbow since 1979.  In 1986 the worker began to feel pain and swelling in his left arm on the inside of his elbow.

The worker suffered a dislocated right thumb in a 1970 work accident.  In 1984, he was awarded a 2.5% pension for osteoarthritis of the first joint of the thumb.  In 1985 the worker sought treatment for pain and triggering of the right hand and investigation disclosed stenosing tenosynovitis in all fingers of his right hand.  Carpal tunnel syndrome in the right hand was diagnosed in 1986.

DecKeywords: Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Maximal medical rehabilitation; Pensions (arrears)
DecSummary: The worker suffered low back and right knee injuries in September 1981.  In December 1984, the Board found that the worker could return to work and discontinued benefits.  The worker did not return to work until March 1985.  In May 1985, the Hearings Officer found no assessable disability to the low back region.  In August 1986, the worker was awarded a 15% pension for low back disability.  The worker appealed to the Tribunal, claiming arrears to the 15% pension.

The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for white finger disease.  The worker was an underground miner from 1955 to 1963.  The Board denied benefits, primarily on the basis of delay in onset of symptoms until 1974.

The worker, who was born in 1923, sought an older worker supplement.  The worker had been a butcher all his life and had poor English language skills.  He received a 30% pension for a low back disability and suffered from other non-compensable conditions.

DecKeywords: Independent operator (truck driver); Right to sue
DecSummary: The plaintiff slipped on ice at the defendant's premises.  The plaintiff owned a truck and entered into an owner/operator agreement with the defendant.  The plaintiff worked exclusively for the defendant.  His truck bore the defendant's logo and the P.V.C. licence was in the defendant's name.  The plaintiff received a set percentage of revenue.  Customers were provided by the defendant.

DecKeywords: Causation (heart attack); Firefighter; Heart attack; Smoking
DecSummary: A 54-year-old firefighter appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a myocardial infarction which occurred at home, 12 hours after completion of an uneventful shift.  The worker had a long history of smoking but there was no known medical history or family history of heart disease.

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (evidence to support Appeal Board conclusion); Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence)
DecSummary: The Appeal Board denied benefits for the worker's bilateral knee disability.  A statement by a manager regarding strain from the nature of the worker's work was not substantial new evidence since the Appeal Board considered both a specific accident and the requirements of the job.  There was evidence to support the Appeal Board conclusion.

The appellant appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for an accident.  The appellant operated a limited company.  He contacted the Board on June 13, 1986, about arranging coverage for employees.  The Board sent out a payroll statement with indication that it should be returned by July 14.  A follow-up notice was sent by the Board on July 28.  The appellant was injured on August 11.  The Board received a copy of the payroll statement on August 27.  The appellant claimed that he mailed the original statement, including coverage for himself, on July 14.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (residual weakness); Delay (onset of symptoms)
DecSummary: The worker suffered compensable low back injuries in 1976 and 1979.  In 1981 he suffered a severe abdominal injury which also was compensable.  The worker claimed that two periods of low back disability in the autumn of 1985 were related to the prior compensable accidents.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Hearing loss
DecSummary: A crane operator had sufficient noise exposure for hearing loss according to  Board guidelines.  Testing in May 1986 found a 36 decibel loss of hearing in one ear and a 35 decibel loss in the other.  Testing in December 1986 found a 30 decibel loss in one ear and only a 20 decibel loss in the other.  The Hearings Officer denied health care benefits for a hearing aid because Board guidelines required a minimum loss of 25 decibels in each ear.

DecKeywords: Discretion, Board (supplements, temporary); Discretion, Board (travel expenses); Leave to appeal (good reason to doubt correctness) (discretion, Board); Supplements, temporary (partial award); Travel expenses (job search)
DecSummary: The worker sought leave to appeal several issues arising from three separate decisions of the Board's Appeal Board.

DecKeywords: Disablement (unaccustomed strain); Recurrences (compensable injury) (strains and sprains)
DecSummary: The worker strained her back in March 1985 and received benefits until her return to work in September 1985.  She laid off again in November 1986 claiming that either there was a recurrence of the 1985 injury or that the nature of her work from August to November 1986 caused a disablement.
The worker was temporarily partially disabled during the period in question.  The Hearings Officer denied full benefits apparently because the worker was unable to provide a job search list.

DecKeywords: Available employment (plant shutdown); Mental condition; Temporary total disability
DecSummary: The worker injured his back in March 1983 and received benefits until October 1983.  In February 1984 the Board determined that the worker continued to be totally disabled and awarded benefits retroactively from October 1983 to February 13, 1984.  The worker returned to modified work on February 14, 1984, but was unable to resume work on a regular basis, despite 15 attempts.  The worker returned to regular hours of work, on modified duties, on June 1, 1984 but was laid off for two weeks in July due to the plant's annual maintenance and vacation shutdown.

The worker was struck in both knees in 1981.  He lost no time from work but spent almost half of the next three years intermittently working at modified employment.  In October 1984 the worker laid off work due to his knee disability and unavailability of modified work with the accident employer.  Extensive medical treatment had not been sought until this time.  The worker's regular employment involved a great deal of walking and climbing.
The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 924/89 was denied.  The evidence supported the conclusions reached in the original decision.  [15 pages]

DecKeywords: Arising out of employment (fighting); Evidence (hearsay); Misconduct (provocation)
DecSummary: The worker appealed the decision of the Hearings Officer denying benefits for injuries suffered in an altercation.  The worker worked on an assembly line producing chairs.  A co-worker injured his finger when a chair frame collapsed.  The co-worker blamed the worker.  An argument ensued.  A supervisor called the worker and co-worker together, the co-worker threatened physical violence, the worker defied the co-worker to do it and the co-worker pushed the worker with the broken chair.

The worker was involved in a compensable accident in April 1976 when he slipped and was prevented from falling by a safety belt.  He underwent a discotomy and returned to work in February 1977.  In March 1983, he suffered a low back strain while moving equipment weighing 70-90 pounds with co-worker.  In July 1983, the worker suffered further back strain while shifting his weight on a motorcycle.

The worker was a dietary helper at a hospital.  She suffered a minor low back strain in October 1982, for which she was off work for about two weeks.  The worker was not entitled to benefits for a lay-off in October 1983.  The 1982 condition related to the mid lumbar area, while the condition in 1983 related to the upper lumbar area.  The 1983 lay-off was not related to the 1982 accident.

DecKeywords: Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Reconsideration (error of law)
DecSummary: While hearing an employer appeal, the Panel decided to broaden the issues under consideration to include the matter of disablement.  In an oral interim decision, the Panel gave the employer the option of proceeding or adjourning.  The employer opted to adjourn.  The employer applied for reconsideration of this interim decision.

The worker applied for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board denying benefits for two accidents in November 1980.  The WCB had investigated but had been unable to find witnesses to corroborate the worker's evidence.  The worker later located a co-worker who had moved away.  Initially, this co-worker was unable to recollect anything about the accident but later provided a signed statement setting out details about condition of machinery and stating that he heard the worker report the accident.

The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 368/89 was denied.  In Decision No. 368/89, the hearing panel denied benefits for degenerative disc disease, finding that the condition was not related to accidents in 1947 and 1961.
